activity: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
knowledge_domain: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
fact: The Collingridge dilemma, from David Collingridge's 1980 book, says a technology's effects are hard to predict when it is new, but by the time they are clear it is hard to change.
story:
Charlie set her fork down before her mother had finished serving the rice, because the phone in her lap had lit up again, and the third message from Van read, "They can't just suspend Oceanne over an app. Can they?"

"Phone away," her mother said, not unkindly, spooning extra chicken onto Charlie's plate as if food could settle any dispute. "You survived an entire childhood without staring at that thing."

"Oceanne got flagged," Charlie said. "By the new system. The one that scores engagement, tracks passes, all of it." Her mother's face did its careful blankness, the look she wore at parent meetings when the school used words like analytics and early intervention. "She's not a troublemaker, Mom. She eats lunch in the library and the algorithm thinks that's avoidance behaviour."

The school had installed the platform in September, and Ms. Xu had been the only teacher to say anything in class, a single dry remark that surveillance was easier to install than to uninstall. Everything else had been effusive, the principal's newsletter practically singing, praising dashboards and data-driven care. Charlie had shrugged along with everyone else. Now Oceanne's name sat on a list, and a meeting had been scheduled for Thursday, and Oceanne had texted Charlie a screenshot of her own score rendered as a colour, a sickly orange, with no explanation of how it had been calculated.

"I want to speak at the meeting," Charlie said, pushing edamame around her plate. "On Thursday. With the parents and the board rep."

Her mother finally sat, hands folded. "You'd stand up in front of all those adults."

"Van and I have been arguing about it all week." Charlie slipped the phone from her lap, thumbing past Van's messages to a note she had been drafting since Sunday. "He says it's already too late, the thing is bought, trained, embedded, that fighting it is revisionist history, trying to rewrite a decision that's already made. Oceanne says the opposite, that it's brand new, barely two months old, and rules can still catch up. They each think the other's crazy."

The story arrived through the screen the way news sometimes does, sideways and half-verified. At the coffee shop on Saturday, Van had pulled up a page on his laptop and turned it toward her. A philosopher of technology, he'd said, a guy named Collingridge, wrote a book in 1980. The idea was later called the Collingridge dilemma: when a technology is new you can't predict its effects, and by the time the effects are clear, you can't change it. "So we're in the gap," Van had said, jabbing the screen. "Nobody knows what this thing does yet, so nobody can argue against it, and in a year it'll be everywhere and untouchable." Oceanne had argued the school was small, it was one platform, it could be voted out. Van had laughed, not cruelly, and said that was exactly what everybody says in the gap.

"Read me what you wrote," her mother said now. It was not a command so much as a trying, and Charlie understood that her mother was offering something, an opening at the table where they usually only discussed grades and bus schedules.

Charlie read aloud, halting at first, then steadier. She had written that the dilemma did not actually say nothing could be done, only that the difficulty was real and came from two directions at once, and that maybe the honest position was to demand transparency without pretending to know outcomes. "Van wants to problematize the whole platform, tear it down rhetorically," she said. "Oceanne wants to reform it, add an appeal process. I keep thinking those aren't opposites, they're two hands doing one job."

"Your grandmother negotiated with a landlord once," her mother said, "with a number she admitted she'd invented. Confidence, not certainty. He never knew."

The phone buzzed against the table. A message from Ms. Xu, of all people, short and careful: "I was told students speaking Thursday may submit a written statement if speaking isn't possible. Three minutes. I would read one aloud if asked. You know what happened to your friend as well as I do, probably better." Charlie stared at the last line. She did know, actually, and here was the fact she had told no one, the one she had been carrying since October: the system had flagged her too, weeks before Oceanne, for the pattern of her Tuesdays, when she left chemistry early to pick up her little brother because their mother worked late. A green badge, a favourable one, had quietly moved her to a "supported independent study" track, and the counsellor had been so pleased, and Charlie had never reported the error because the error was kind to her. The algorithm had misread her life and given her a gift, and she had let it stand.

She typed a reply to Ms. Xu, then deleted it, then typed again, and finally showed her mother the screen before sending. "I'll speak," it said. "I was flagged too, in the other direction. I'll say that." Her mother read it twice, the kitchen timer ticking down toward something in the oven, her thumb resting on the edge of the screen as if the message might still be taken back.

"Send it," her mother said.

Charlie pressed send, and the little delivered mark appeared, and she picked up her fork.

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: In the United States and many other countries, a play is protected by copyright automatically as soon as it is written down, without needing to be registered.
story:
Ethan sat cross-legged on his bedroom floor with the laptop warm on his thighs and a legal pad beside him, on which he had written, three days running, the same first stage direction: A kitchen. Two chairs. Late. He was supposed to have a ten-minute play drafted by Friday for the young writers' showcase at the community theatre, and the play was supposed to be about a moment from his own life, which was the part that kept stopping him. His life, as far as he could tell, consisted mostly of moments he hadn't understood while they were happening.

He tried anyway. He wrote the scene he kept circling: the night his father came home from the hospital in February, thin and slow, and ate half a bowl of soup before falling asleep at the table, and how Ethan had sat across from him not saying anything, listening to the refrigerator hum. It had taken months for his father to recuperate, and during that time nobody in the house had discussed it directly, which was maybe why the scene felt both urgent and impossible. He wrote four lines of dialogue, read them aloud in a whisper, and heard immediately that they were false. Nobody in his family announced their feelings. They passed the salt.

His phone buzzed against the carpet. It was Enzo, who was also in the showcase, in a state of panic that seemed, from the frequency of his messages, to be self-sustaining. "I'm not sending my script to the organizer," the message read. "What if he steals it. It's the best thing I've written." Ethan laughed, then stopped, because he realized he had been quietly worried about the same thing. His play had his family in it, barely disguised. If someone took it and staged it somewhere, it wouldn't just be theft of words. It would be his kitchen, his father, passed around.

Florence had told him once that his caution was ridiculous, that nobody wanted anyone else's ten-minute play badly enough to steal it, but Ethan wanted to check for himself. He typed "is a play protected by copyright" into the search bar, expecting a maze of forms and fees, some official registration he'd have to complete before Friday. The first result made him sit up straight. In the United States and many other countries, the page said, a play is protected by copyright automatically as soon as it is written down, without needing to be registered.

He read it twice, then texted Enzo: "You don't have to register it. It's copyrighted the moment you write it down. Here and in a lot of other countries." He could almost hear the exhale from across town. The reply came back as a single crying-laughing face, and then, "so it's already mine," and Ethan looked at the legal pad and thought, with a small strange thrill, that the false four lines of dialogue he'd written an hour ago already belonged to him, legally, in their falseness. Nobody could take them. Only he could fix them.

He called Mr. O'Brien, who lived two doors down and had directed the showcase for eleven years, and asked whether he could stage the play with almost no dialogue. "Two people at a table," Ethan said, "and one of them mostly silent." There was a pause on the line that Ethan had learned not to fear; Mr. O'Brien's pauses were where he did his thinking. "Silence is very hard," he said finally. "The audience will fill it with whatever they bring. Are you prepared for that?" Ethan said he thought so, and found, saying it, that he half meant it.

He worked until nearly midnight, stripping the scene back. What remained was the soup, the passing of bread, the son watching, and at the end a sound cue he notated carefully: the refrigerator hum rising and then fading, a diminuendo that took the last thirty seconds of the play down into the kitchen's ordinary noise. Whether that was an ending or just a stopping, he genuinely didn't know. His mother put her head around the door at eleven to ask if he wanted tea, read three lines over his shoulder without comment, and left the mug where he could reach it. That, he thought, was probably the truest review he would get.

On Friday the little theatre smelled of dust and the noxious ghost of fresh paint from the lobby renovation, and Ethan sat in the third row while Enzo's play went first, and then his own. The two chairs, the table, the actor playing his father eating slowly. Somewhere behind him, an audience member shifted and sighed, filling the silence with her own kitchen, whoever's it was. When the hum faded out and the lights went down, nobody clapped for a full second, and Ethan spent that second not breathing, listening to what other people had brought.

Then the applause, and Florence turning around in the row ahead, mouthing, "Is that your dad?"

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: The CDC advises against washing raw chicken, because the splashing water can spread bacteria to the sink and nearby surfaces.
story:
Jayden turned on the tap and held the split chicken under it the way his grandmother had done every Sunday of his childhood, water drumming against the skin, a thin pink river crawling toward the drain. Across the counter, Sofia reached over and shut the faucet off with the flat of her hand.

"Don't," she said. "The CDC says not to wash raw chicken. The splashing water spreads bacteria to the sink and everything near it."

Jayden stood there with wet hands. He wanted to say something about his grandmother, whose hands had done this ten thousand times, whose kitchen in his memory smelled of lime and char and whose methods were, to him, a kind of patrimony, passed down like the cast iron pan nobody was allowed to scrub with soap. Instead he said, "You're kidding."

"Look it up yourself."

Ms. Hoang was walking the rows of stations with her clipboard, and the clock above the door read 2:41. They had nineteen minutes to get the tray into the oven, because the whole point of today was the family meal demonstration, the dish he had promised his mother he would bring home intact for dinner tonight, his first real contribution after eightteen years of being fed. He had planned it around the chicken his mother had dropped off that morning, cold and wrapped in a grocery bag.

He dried his hands and pulled out his phone, thumbs working fast. Sofia was right. He read it twice, half aloud, and Micah leaned over from the pasta station to hear.

"So all those years," Micah said.

"All those years."

The problem was not that his grandmother had been wrong, exactly. She had cooked in a kitchen with one cutting board and no thermometer and nobody had ever gotten sick, or nobody had ever said so, which might be the same thing. But Sofia's phone had the government website on it and the government website had no memory of anyone's grandmother at all. Jayden found he couldn't make these two things lie flat against each other. His grandmother's practice and the CDC's warning were both, as far as he could tell, true, and they sutured together only badly, like two edges of skin that keep pulling apart when you try to close them. He patted the chicken dry with paper towels instead, which felt like a small betrayal performed with clean hands.

"Twelve minutes," Ms. Hoong called, and Jayden realized he had not salted it yet, had not oiled the pan, had done nothing but stand there holding a paper towel and thinking about kitchens he could not reconcile. Sofia slid the sheet pan toward him without comment. He oiled it. He salted the chicken, more than he thought he needed, less than his grandmother would have used, and settled the pieces skin side up, and the oven took the tray with a rush of heat that touched his face.

"You okay?" Sofia asked. She was a mercurial person, sharp one minute and quiet the next, and he never knew which he was getting until she opened her mouth.

"I'm going to tell my mom," he said. "When she asks why I didn't rinse it. I'm going to tell her what I read."

"She'll fight you on it."

"Probably." He wiped down the sink anyway, all of it, the handles and the backsplash, working outward from the drain the way the website had described, and wondered whether he was being careful or just obedient, whether there was a difference his grandmother would have recognized. He could already hear his mother: we've done it this way forever. He could already hear himself: the CDC advises against it. Two sentences, both true, aimed at each other across a kitchen that wasn't this one.

The timer on his station beeped once to mark the halfway point. Through the oven door the skin had gone pale gold at the edges, not yet blistered. Ms. Hoang paused at their station and made a mark on her clipboard and moved on without saying anything, which was somehow worse than a correction.

Micah called over, "Jayden, your phone's going off."

It was his mother, and the screen said 2:56, and dinner was at six. He picked it up, still watching the chicken through the glass. "Hey," he said. "I'm not going to rinse it. I'll explain when I get home."

activity: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
knowledge_domain: to find the derivative of a polynomial function and use it to locate a maximum
fact: By the first derivative test, a point where the derivative changes from positive to negative is a local maximum, because the function rises and then falls.
story:
The kitchen table smelled of oregano and pencil shavings, and Rose had claimed the good end of it, the end without the wobble, because she intended to win an argument. Hayley sat across from her with a shoebox of fundraiser candles and the expression of someone who had already decided the matter. Behind them Rose's father dried dishes and said, to no one in particular, that the car loan would amortize over five years and that this was a thing Rose would eventually have to care about, which she doubted.

"Ten dollars a candle," Hayley said. "That's the price. Done."

"You're guessing," Rose said. She had Hayley's sales sheet in front of her, three weeks of it, and she had spent the bus ride home turning the columns into a function, revenue depending on price, the way Ms. Bekele had made them do with the popcorn problem before anyone understood why. "There's a way to actually know."

Hayley's mother, delivering a plate of biscotti, was effusive in a way that made Rose suspect she had overheard none of it. "Look at you two, studying on a Friday. My Hayley never studies on a Friday." Hayley waited until her mother had retreated to the stove, then slid the sales sheet back toward Rose with two fingers, as though it might be contagious.

"Fine. Know it, then."

Rose turned over a napkin. On the left she drew a number line for the price and marked the point where the derivative came out to zero, the point Hayley's own numbers were circling. To the left of it she wrote a plus sign, because when she checked the derivative there it came out positive, and to the right she wrote a minus sign, because there it came out negative. She tapped the point in the middle. "It's called the first derivative test," she said, and then, because Hayley's face had gone politely blank, "the function rises up to here and then falls after. Rising, then falling. That's a peak. That's where your money stops going up and starts going down."

"That's what a graph is for," Hayley said, but she leaned in anyway, and Baby, who had come for the biscotti and stayed for the dispute, leaned in from the side like a person watching tennis.

"A graph shows you one guess," Rose said. In her other class they were writing about logos, the appeal to reason, and she was beginning to suspect that a sign chart on a napkin was the purest logos anyone had ever put in front of Hayley, though she would not have said so out loud. "This works for the whole thing. It doesn't care what the graph looks like. Your best price is before ten. Below ten you're rising, above ten you're falling, so your maximum is right there at the point in the middle."

Baby reached across and traced the plus and minus signs with a biscotti-dusted finger. "So she's been leaving money on the table."

"The table," Hayley said, with dignity, "is where we eat."

But she took the napkin. She held it up to the light, frowning at it the way her mother frowned at expired coupons, and Rose watched her check the plus sign, then the minus sign, then the little peak drawn between them. "You're sure the signs aren't backwards," Hayley said. "You're sure it's not a valley."

"If it fell and then rose, it would be a valley. This rises and then falls. That's the whole difference."

Baby, who had a calculus quiz Monday and had until this moment treated the subject as a rumor, asked to see it again, and Rose watched her friend's face do the thing faces do when a door opens somewhere behind the eyes. Baby copied the number line onto her arm with a pen. Hayley's mother called out asking whether anyone wanted more biscotti, and Hayley said no without turning around.

"I'll think about the price," Hayley said at last, which Rose understood to mean she would not think about the price. That was fine. Hayley folded the napkin anyway, small, then smaller, and put it in the pocket of her hoodie, and when Baby reached for it Hayley moved her hand away without looking up and said, "Get your own derivative."

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A standard piano has 88 keys: 52 white and 36 black.
story:
The piano had stood in his grandmother's front room since before Oliver was born, and in all those years he had never once touched it. He had played trumpet in the school band instead, badly, sitting in the back row where Mr. Smith could pretend not to notice. But after the funeral in March, when the house passed to his parents and they began sorting through the rooms with a spartan efficiency that frightened him, Oliver found himself drawn to the bench every evening. He didn't have a reason he could defend. He only knew that when his hands were on the keys, the house still sounded like her.

He commandeered the front room as his practice space, hauling the boxes of china and linens into the hall so the piano could breathe. There was no money for lessons, so he worked from a beginner's book he found in the bench, a relic with someone else's pencil marks in the margins. His progress was slow and specific: two measures of a Bach minuet by the second week, four by the fourth, his left hand lagging behind his right like a reluctant brother.

Saad came by on a Saturday in June, ostensibly to help move furniture, actually to avoid his own packing for college. He dropped onto the couch and watched Oliver stumble through the minuet twice. "How many of those things are there?" he asked, nodding at the keyboard. "The keys."

"Fifty-two white," Oliver said, and then he stopped playing, because he realized he wasn't certain about the rest. He had counted the white ones one afternoon, a task that took ten minutes and felt absurd the whole time. "Thirty-six black. Eighty-eight total." He said it with the small pride of someone who has verified something no one asked him to verify, and Saad laughed, but not unkindly.

"You counted them."

"I was waiting for my phone to charge."

Saad crossed to the piano and ran a finger along the black keys, the uneven clusters, two and three, repeating like a pattern in a carpet. "It's a weird number," he said. "You'd think it'd be round." He pressed one, then another. "Play me the thing again. The minuet." Oliver played it, and this time he got through all eight measures without stopping, and Saad, who had heard him murder trumpet fanfares for three years, said nothing at all, which was the highest compliment he knew how to give.

In the kitchen, the grandfather listened to the minuet through the wall. He had said little since March, answering questions in fragments, taking his coffee out to the porch alone. He had never learned to play the instrument himself; his wife had been the pianist, and he had been the audience, and it had never occurred to him until now that those might be unequal positions. He heard the boy stop, start over, stop again. He heard the particular stubbornness in it, a rectitude about the small notes that reminded him of her, of the way she would repeat a single passage until the neighbors probably wondered whether the record had skipped. He dried his hands on the dish towel and stood in the doorway of the front room.

"You're rushing the third beat," he said. Both boys turned. "She did that too, when she was learning something. Rushing."

"You know this piece?" Oliver asked.

"She played it forty years." The old man came to the bench and looked at the keys as if greeting a crowd of acquaintances. "Eighty-eight of them," he said. "Fifty-two white and thirty-six black. She told me that on our second date, at a hotel lobby piano. I thought it was the most useless thing anyone had ever said to me." He did not sit down. "It isn't, though. You count them, you know what you have. Then you stop counting."

Saad quietly gathered his jacket from the couch and let himself out the front door, and the screen hinge announced it. Oliver shifted on the bench to make room, uncertain whether the invitation would be understood as an invitation. His grandfather stood a moment longer, then lowered himself onto the far end of the bench, his hands flat on his knees.

"Play it," the old man said. "From the top."

Oliver set his fingers on the keys, fifty-two white, thirty-six black, and began.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: Supporters of lowering the US voting age to 18 used the slogan "old enough to fight, old enough to vote," because 18-year-olds could be drafted for the Vietnam War.
story:
The registration form sat on the desk in front of Riley like a test he hadn't studied for, though it was only nine boxes and a signature line. Mr. He had set the stack on the front table before the bell and said, almost offhand, that anyone turning eighteen before November could fill one out now, that the county clerk would be there Thursday. Riley's birthday was in eleven days. He had done the math twice on the margin of his notebook, once in pen.

"So you're actually going to do it," Bruce said from the seat behind him, leaning forward over Riley's shoulder. Bruce had a way of making questions sound like verdicts. "You know your one vote is mathematically nothing, right? Like, actually nothing."

"It's not nothing if everyone thinks that," Riley said.

"Everyone does think that. That's my point." Bruce sat back, satisfied, and started doodling a rocket on his folder.

Felix, on Riley's other side, hadn't said anything. He was reading the form itself, the actual text, mouthing the residency question. Felix read everything, including cereal boxes, including terms of service. Riley slid his chair a few inches toward him and asked, quietly, whether the party affiliation box could be left blank. Felix said it could. Felix said you could also register and then never vote at all, and nobody would come to your door.

The classroom was warm for October. Mr. He had propped the window six inches and the traffic on Delancey came through in slow waves, a bus sighing, then nothing, then a delivery truck. On the board, in his cramped vertical handwriting, was the homework: an essay on a right that expanded during your parents' lifetime, three pages, due Monday. Riley had stared at it Sunday night and written nothing, because the only right he could think of in a personal way was the one arriving at his desk on a clipboard.

At dinner that night his father asked, in the flat tone he used for things he cared about, whether Riley had decided. Riley said he was deciding, and his father said that was the wrong answer, that men had decided for him long enough and eighteen meant he stopped being decided for. His grandfather, visiting from Harrisburg, looked up from his soup with a saturnine expression, like the whole conversation was weather he had been caught in before.

"Can I ask why it's eighteen at all?" Riley said. "Why not twenty-one? It used to be twenty-one, right?"

His grandfather set down the spoon. He spoke the way he paid for things, counting out each word. "During Vietnam, eighteen-year-olds could be drafted. So the people pushing to lower the voting age had a slogan. Old enough to fight, old enough to vote." He picked the spoon back up. "That's where it came from."

Nobody said anything for a moment. Riley's father refilled the water glasses with unnecessary care.

"They couldn't vote for the people sending them," Riley said slowly.

"Correct," his grandfather said, and that was all he said about it, which for him was a speech.

Riley stayed at the table after the others drifted to the kitchen, turning his glass a quarter turn at a time. Bruce was right about the arithmetic; one vote had never decided anything Riley could name. His father was right about the principle, though his father was right about principles the way he was right about mortgage rates, loudly and without curiosity. What sat in front of Riley was neither the arithmetic nor the principle but something between them, the way a crowd moves because each person in it moves a little.

Thursday, the clerk came. She was a small woman with a lanyard and a rolling suitcase of forms, and she set up at the front table while Mr. He took attendance. Felix went first, out of some private orderliness, and came back looking faintly ceremonial. Bruce didn't move, and when Mr. He raised an eyebrow at him, Bruce said, "Civic mutualism only works if everyone joins, and I'm performing my individual right not to," which was a sentence Riley could hear him constructing even as he said it. Mr. He, unbothered, wrote something in his attendance book.

Riley walked the form up himself. The clerk checked his birthdate against her list, asked him to print his name, and turned the page for the signature. His hand hesitated over the line for a second, not out of doubt exactly, more the awareness that the signature would be his from now on, the one he would use on leases and taxes and everything after.

He signed. She stapled his receipt and said, "You'll get a card in the mail," and he carried the little yellow slip back to his seat like change from a purchase he couldn't return.

"What did that catalyze in you," Bruce said, deadpan, "enlightenment? A sense of oneness with the republic?"

Riley looked at the slip. He thought about his grandfather counting out the words, about eighteen-year-olds who had been handed rifles and not ballots, and he thought about the bus sighing on Delancey, and he found he couldn't make those into one clean feeling and didn't much want to.

"I don't know yet," he said. "Ask me in November."

Felix leaned over and tapped the yellow slip once, gently, the way you'd tap a screen door to see if it was real.

"You still don't know who you're voting for," Felix said.

"No," Riley said. "But I know I get to."

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: At the top of its path a projectile's vertical velocity is zero, but its horizontal velocity is not, so it is still moving.
story:
The worksheet had twelve problems, and Sienna had solved none of them by the time the bell rang for lunch. Each one showed a ball, a cannonball, a slightly suicidal snowmobile, launched at some angle, and asked where it would be after so many seconds. She understood the equations individually. What she could not see was how to hold two motions in one object at the same time, like trying to sing a round alone.

"You're staring at it like it insulted your family," said Erika, sliding her tray onto the table across from Sienna. Behind her, Beatrice was arguing with the cafeteria cashier about whether a bagel counted as a bakery item or a bread item, an argument she lost every day and restarted every day, a peccadillo the cashier had long since habituated himself to, judging by the flatness of his sigh.

"It insulted my intelligence," Sienna said. "Problem four. A ball thrown at an angle. They want the velocity at the top of its path, and I keep getting zero, but the answer key says it's not zero, and I don't understand how something can be at the top and still be moving. The top is where you stop. That's what a top is."

Erika picked up the worksheet, read it upside down, and turned it right side up with visible effort. "Maybe the answer key is wrong."

"Maybe I'm wrong."

"That's the boring option," said Erika, though she said it kindly, and Beatrice arrived with her bagel and a sardonic observation about the pricing taxonomy of the cafeteria, and the conversation moved on, but Sienna kept the worksheet on the table beside her sandwich, half of which she forgot to eat.

That afternoon was physics with Mr. Johansson, a man who had once, memorably, dropped a bowling ball off the bleachers while wearing safety goggles and a raincoat, for reasons he declined to state afterward. Today he wrote one sentence on the board and underlined it twice: components. "Your homework," he said, gathering his coffee, "is to convince yourselves." Then he left the room, which was his way, and the class sat there with the word underlined twice and no further instruction.

Components. Sienna wrote it in her margin and sat with it. If you split a velocity, the way you'd split a bill, then the sideways part of the ball and the up-and-down part were, what, separate accounts? She drew a right triangle with the thrown ball's speed as the long side, then the two legs. The horizontal leg, the vertical leg. Separate accounts. The vertical one was the one that fought gravity, slowed, hit its peak. The horizontal one had nothing fighting it. It just kept going.

She was still turning the triangle around in her notebook when Beatrice sat down beside her, because the seat had emptied and Beatrice liked windows. "What's the triangle for?"

"Problem four," Sienna said. "I think I think the ball never stops at the top. Vertically it stops, but sideways it doesn't. It's still moving, just flat."

Beatrice frowned, which on Beatrice was a whole facial event. "At the top, it stops. I've seen balls. They hang there."

"Where?"

"Volleyball. Every game."

Sienna considered this. She had watched volleyball for years and would have sworn to the same thing, that half-instant where the ball seemed pinned to the air. "Can we look?"

They looked. Beatrice had, for reasons involving her brother and a broken promise, a folder of slow-motion volleyball videos on her phone, and they scrolled through them in the back of the room while Mr. Johansson's coffee lasted, and there it was, frame by frame. The ball rose, and the rise drained out of it, and at the very top of its arc it hung, no height left to gain, and yet the ball was not still in the frame, it had shifted, clearly, measurably sideways, from one frame to the next, traveling flat across the sky like something crossing a corridor.

"Wait," Beatrice said. She scrubbed back two frames and held the phone where Sienna could see. "So at the top its vertical velocity is zero."

"But its horizontal velocity isn't," Sienna said. "It's still moving."

They watched it again. Beatrice, who argued with cashiers for sport, did not argue with the video.

In the fall, before any of this, Sienna had gone with her mother to a county fair and watched a man in a tricorne hat launch pumpkins from a trebuchet, and she remembered standing at the rope line wondering why the pumpkins seemed to flatten out at the top of their arc, like birds deciding to glide. She had thought it was her eyes. She had thought a lot of things were her eyes that year. She mentioned the pumpkins now and Beatrice said that trebuchets were superior to catapults and that this was non-negotiable, and Sienna laughed, and then, under the underlined word, she redid problem four.

It took four lines. Vertical velocity at the top: zero, which she now understood was only half a sentence. Horizontal velocity: whatever the sideways leg of the triangle was, unchanged, cruising along as if nothing had happened to its dramatic sibling. She wrote the answer the key wanted, and then she wrote it again in her own handwriting, slower, the way you'd copy a sentence from a language you were just starting to speak.

Erika leaned over from the next row. "So was the answer key right or were you right?"

"Both of us were half right," Sienna said. "The ball stops going up. It doesn't stop going."

"Huh," said Erika, and looked, for a moment, like someone who had just noticed the window was open in a room she'd been sitting in all year. Then she borrowed Sienna's calculator without asking, as she always did, and Sienna let her, as she always did, and outside the window a pigeon crossed the sky in a long, level glide, and Sienna watched it all the way to the flagpole.

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: Molar mass in grams per mole has the same number as a particle's average mass in atomic mass units; one carbon atom averages about 12.01 units, and one mole of carbon about 12.01 grams.
story:
The room smelled like the janitor had mopped with something faintly arboreal, pine in a bottle, and Sebastian sat with the worksheet Ms. Oyelaran had left for the substitute to distribute, three problems about grams of methane burning into grams of carbon dioxide. He had gotten the first one wrong twice. The second time he had forgotten to balance the equation, which felt like a personal failure, since balancing was the part he could actually do.

"Sixteen grams of methane," said Bastien, reading over his shoulder without being invited. "You're going to want the molar mass on that one."

"I know what I want." Sebastian covered his paper with his forearm, an old reflex from years of shared desks. "I'm getting there."

Bastien's whole ambition this semester was to be first in the class, not out of any love of chemistry, which he described as "fine," but because his older brother had been first and their mother mentioned it at dinner with a frequency that had passed from flattering to liturgical. He had already finished his own worksheet. He had finished it, Sebastian suspected, partly to have time left over to watch other people not finish theirs.

The trouble was the middle step. Sebastian could read the mass off the problem, and he could find the molar mass under carbon on the periodic table, 12.01, and he could see oxygen's number too, but the bridge between a pile of grams and a number of moles kept collapsing. He wrote 12.01 on the margin of his page and stared at it. Then he flipped to the periodic table taped above the sink and stared at the same number there, printed under C in a small square, described in the caption as the average mass of a single atom, in atomic mass units. One atom. 12.01 units. And one mole of carbon, according to the chart on the side wall, was 12.01 grams. The same number, doing both jobs.

He turned back around slowly, the way you do when you suspect the room has rearranged itself behind you.

"Sam," he said, to the girl two seats over who was drawing a cat on her folder, "come here a second."

Sam came, because Sam collected other people's crises the way some people collect stamps. She stood at his shoulder and he pointed at the 12.01 under carbon. "That's for one atom," he said, "and it's also for a whole mole of it. Same number. One atom averages 12.01 units, and a mole of it is 12.01 grams." He had expected her to be unimpressed, but she leaned in and checked the side chart herself, mouthing the word grams.

"That's either a coincidence," she said, "or the laziest thing I've ever seen chemistry do."

"It's not a coincidence," said Bastien from across the aisle, with the mild superiority of someone who had known this since Tuesday. Sebastian ignored him, partly on principle and partly because Bastien being right was, at this moment, useful, and Sebastian was honest enough with himself to note the tension in that. He wrote methane's molar mass by adding the numbers, then divided the sixteen grams by it, and the grams cancelled on the page the way Ms. Oyelaran had shown them in September, units striking through like items crossed off a list. Sixteen grams of methane was about one mole of methane. And one mole of methane, the balanced equation said, made one mole of carbon dioxide. So he multiplied that mole count by the molar mass of carbon dioxide, and a number of grams appeared, and it had units and everything.

"Seventeen thousand," he said, then looked again. "No. Forty-four grams. Roughly." He had read his own handwriting wrong, interpolating between the four and the six as if his notes were a smooth curve rather than a string of mistakes. He crossed it out.

Bastien drifted over with his finished worksheet, ostensibly to sharpen his pencil at the sharpener near the window, and hovered. "You could check it against mine," he said.

"I don't want to check it against yours."

"You want to check it against a dilettante, then," Bastien said, indicating Sam, who raised her cat-decorated folder as a shield. "Someone who's only here for the drama."

"I'm here for the cat," Sam confirmed.

But Sebastian did want to check it, and he was aware that refusing to check it against Bastien's paper was less about integrity than about not handing Bastien the satisfaction. He weighed this for a moment, the actual value of being right against the cost of admitting Bastien could help. Then he slid his paper across the aisle, face up, an offering. "Just the setup. Don't tell me the answer."

Bastien looked at it for a long four seconds. "Your setup's right," he said, and there was something reluctant in it, as if the answer had cost him more than the words admitted. He went back to his seat and began, without announcing it, redoing his own third problem. He erased the whole line and started over. Sebastian watched him do it and did not say anything, and neither did Sam, who was watching too.

At the front of the room the substitute had fallen asleep with her chin on her fist, or was performing an extremely committed impression of it. Outside, someone's physical education class ran laps around the track, and the sound of it came through the window in soft, regular surges.

Ms. Oyelaran came back for the last ten minutes, carrying her coffee and a stack of handouts she'd clearly forgotten to leave. She walked the rows once, paused at Sebastian's page, tapped the margin where he'd written 12.01 twice with two arrows pointing at it from either side, and said, "Nice."

"Is it right?" Sebastian asked.

"It's a good question," she said, and kept walking, which was either a compliment or a dodge, and he decided, while there was still time to decide, not to ask which. He copied his number onto the fresh sheet, boxed it, and drew the arrows again, bigger.

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: On level ground with no air resistance, a launch angle of 45 degrees gives the greatest range for a given launch speed.
story:
The garage smelled of cut pine and cold metal, and the ball launcher sat on the workbench like something half finished, which it was. Rhiannon had welded the frame; Haiden had wired the trigger; Laurence had spent three evenings failing to make a tennis ball go where she wanted. The county science fair was in nine days, and the distance contest had a trophy that their rival school had taken home two years running.

"Thirty degrees again," Haiden said, marking the landing spot with chalk on the concrete floor. "Fourteen and a half feet."

Rhiannon bent over the tape measure, wrote the number in the notebook, and looked at Laurence. "You said the math would fix this."

Laurence had said that. She had the textbook open on a milk crate, the chapter on projectile motion, and the whole idea of it had beguiled her at first reading: the horizontal part of the motion and the vertical part could be treated as if they lived separate lives, one steady, one falling. Nothing in her geometry class had prepared her for a thing being two things at once. But when she tried to turn the pages into the machine, the numbers slid away from her. She could say the words. She could not yet make them mean anything.

"It will," she said.

The house behind the garage belonged to Ms. Santoso, who had let them use it since her husband died and left it full of tools nobody used. She came out on the third evening with a plate of sliced mango and stood in the doorway, arms folded, watching the ball thump against the far wall.

"You're doing the launch contest," she said. It wasn't a question. "My husband judged it for years. The team from Fairview always won." She set the plate on the crate, next to the textbook, and tapped the page with one finger, right on the diagram. Then she went back inside without another word, and Laurence stared at the diagram she had already stared at for hours: the arrow split into two arrows, one flat along the ground, one straight up.

"It's the same speed," she said out loud, mostly to herself. "Whatever angle you launch at, the speed is the speed. The angle just decides how you divide it."

"So pick a division," Rhiannon said.

"It's not a division. It's a trade." Laurence drew it in the notebook margin, a shallow line, a steep line. Flat, the ball hurried along the ground and died quickly. Steep, it climbed beautifully and came down almost where it started. Somewhere between the two there had to be a best, and the textbook, when she flipped the page, gave it without argument: forty-five degrees. On level ground with no air resistance, the greatest range came at forty-five.

"No air resistance," Haiden said, reading over her shoulder. "This garage is full of air."

"So we test it." Laurence loosened the wing nut on the launcher's pivot arm and set the protractor against it. Forty-five. The first ball went twenty-one feet, chalk mark well past every earlier mark. Rhiannon whooped. They ran it at forty and at fifty, the way Laurence insisted, writing each number down, and both marks fell short of the forty-five mark by inches.

"It's true," Rhiannon said. "Forty-five wins."

"On level ground with no air," Laurence said. "The floor here is level. The gymnasium floor at the fair is level. The ball's not very light, so air shouldn't beguile us into thinking it matters more than it does." She frowned at her own sentence. "Shouldn't fool us, I mean. The tennis ball's heavy enough."

"Say beguile," Haiden said. "It's a better word. My elocution coach would approve."

"You don't have an elocution coach."

"My mother does. Same thing in our house."

Laurence laughed for the first time in three evenings, and then stopped, because the problem was still on the bench. The contest rules gave each team two launches, best one counted. Forty-five was the best angle for the machine as it stood, but the machine's spring was tired; Haiden had found a stronger one at the indigent end of a salvage bin, two dollars, and if they swapped it in, every number they had would change. The angle might not change. She believed the forty-five held regardless of speed; the textbook had said for a given launch speed, which meant each speed had its own forty-five. But she hadn't proven anything, and the fair was in five days.

They installed the new spring by flashlight, Ms. Santoso's porch light having gone off at ten. Rhiannon cranked the arm back. It clicked louder, held harder.

"Forty-five," Laurence said, checking the protractor twice. "Fire."

The ball hit the far wall above the door, hard enough to leave a smear of chalk, and dropped somewhere they couldn't see.

"Get the tape," Rhiannon said, already running for the door.

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: The US Telecommunications Act of 1996 eliminated the national cap on radio station ownership, and the number of station owners then fell sharply even as the number of stations grew.
story:
William had noticed it in June, on the drive to his grandmother's house in Ohio, and it had bothered him all summer. The radio in Cincinnati was playing the same talk show, with the same host laughing at the same caller, that his father listened to in their own city three hundred miles away. Not a similar show. The same one, down to the advertisements for a mattress chain that had no stores near either place. He kept wondering how that could happen, the way you keep turning a strange key in your pocket.

On the first Tuesday of school he found his chance. Ms. Bélanger had assigned a short paper for civics, one paragraph on any question about "how information reaches people." Most of the class groaned. William went to the public library after last period, chose a carrel near the window where the late light came through in a long rectangle, and spread his notebook open. The question he wrote at the top was simple: why do two cities get the same radio?

Brianne found him there twenty minutes later, carrying a smoothie and looking for a place to sit. She leaned over his shoulder. "That's your topic? Radio?"

"Two cities, same show," William said. "Same host, same ads, everything. Like it's one station wearing two coats."

"That's just syndication," she said. "Shows get sold to lots of stations."

"That's what my dad said. But it's not just the shows. It's the news too. Cincinnati's local news was read by somebody in a studio somewhere else, and I don't think she'd ever been to Cincinnati." He turned the notebook toward her. "I want to know who actually owns these stations. Not who talks on them. Who owns them."

The library's computers were the old slow kind, and the business database made him log in twice, but the searching itself was the good part, the feeling of a question loosening like a knot. He found a trade magazine article from the 1990s, its pages scanned crookedly. He read a line, sat back, read it again. Then he said, out loud and too loud, "Nineteen ninety-six."

Ainsley, two seats over with a calculus book, shushed him without looking up. Brianne slid her chair around. William pointed at the screen. "The Telecommunications Act of 1996. It eliminated the national cap on radio station ownership. So before that, there was a limit on how many stations one company could own across the whole country. After it, no limit."

"Which means what?"

He scrolled, hunting, and the numbers came up in a chart with tiny print he had to lean close to read. The article said the number of station owners then fell sharply, even as the number of stations grew. He copied both facts into his notebook, then read them back to make sure he hadn't flipped anything. More stations, fewer owners. It sounded like a truism turned inside out, the kind of thing that should have been obvious and wasn't. "So my dad's station and my grandmother's station are probably owned by the same company," he said. "That's why they sound the same. It's not a coincidence. Somebody decided."

"Decided what, though?" Brianne asked. "To play a mattress ad?"

"To make both stations cheap to run, I think. One newsroom for ten cities instead of ten newsrooms." He hesitated, because he could feel himself running ahead of what he actually knew. "I don't know that part. The article doesn't say why the owners fell. It just says they did."

He went looking for why, and that was where it got harder. One editorial called the consolidation a disaster, another called it the natural efficiency of the market, and both were so doctrinaire, so sealed against doubt, that he trusted neither. He found a legal column that spent a full page on a licensing dispute in which the company had agreed to indemnify its subsidiaries against fines, and he understood from the surrounding sentences that this meant the parent company would cover the losses, would take the penalty on itself. Which meant, he thought, writing it down, that the people talking on the air were not the people responsible for what the station did. The responsibility sat somewhere upstairs, in a building he would never see.

He wrote his paragraph twice. The first version was angry, and he crossed it out. The second said that the same company could own stations in cities far apart, that a law had removed the national cap on ownership in 1996, that owners fell sharply afterward while stations kept growing, and that this had changed what a listener heard without the listener ever being told. Then he added one more sentence, which he almost deleted: what he still didn't know was whether the owners chose the news on purpose, or whether sameness just happened, the way water runs downhill because nobody built a wall. Both were possible. He left the sentence in.

Ms. Bélanger read it the next morning and wrote a single word in the margin, a word William didn't look up until lunch: good. But what he kept thinking about was the drive home in October, when his father turned on the familiar station and the familiar host came on, laughing at a caller from somewhere far away. William watched the signal bars on the dashboard and said, "Dad, did you know this station's owned by a company in another state?"

His father kept his eyes on the road. "Since when do you care who owns the radio?"

"Since I found out," William said, and reached over and turned the volume down, just slightly, so he could hear himself think.

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: The US Consumer Financial Protection Bureau notes a typical payday loan fee of $15 per $100 borrowed for two weeks equals an annual percentage rate of almost 400 percent.
story:
The automatic doors of First Regional split open with a sigh, and Elijah held the door an extra beat for a woman balancing a toddler on one hip. He had come to open his first savings account, the one his mother had been nudging him toward since he started his job at the garden centre, and he carried the deposit slip in his fist like a hall pass. Sarah was already inside, sitting on the bench by the teller windows with her backpack hugged to her chest, which was how she sat when something was wrong.

"You're early," he said. "You're never early."

"I need to ask you something, and I didn't want to do it at school." She kept her voice low, though the branch was nearly empty, just a man filling out a slip at the island of pens chained to the counter. "Rent's due Friday. I'm two hundred short. My hours got cut and I thought I'd be fine, and then the car, and." She stopped. "There's a place on Marsh Street. Payday loans. The sign says fifteen dollars per hundred."

Elijah sat down beside her. Fifteen dollars per hundred did not sound like much; that was the trouble with it. He took out his phone and opened the calculator, thumbing in numbers while she watched. "Fifteen per hundred for two weeks," he said. "That's what it is, right? Two weeks?"

"Two weeks, then you pay it back."

He worked it out, and then worked it out again because the answer seemed wrong. He turned the screen toward her. If the fee were carried across a whole year, that same fifteen per hundred came to an annual percentage rate of almost 400 percent. He'd read that figure on the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's site last month, when he'd been trying to understand credit cards, and the calculator had just reproduced it on its own.

Sarah stared at the number. "Four hundred percent."

"Almost," Elijah said. "The CFPB's the one that says it. So if you can't pay it back in two weeks, and you roll it over, you're not borrowing two hundred anymore. You're borrowing two hundred plus thirty, and then it borrows you."

"That's not a real sentence," she said, but she almost smiled, and then she pressed her palms into her eyes. "So what do I do? I don't have it. They'll charge a late fee at my place, and my mom would give it to me but she doesn't have it either, and I already asked once this year."

Elijah looked past her at the teller windows, at the little brochure rack near the door where he'd been standing five minutes ago. On the savings side of the rack there had been a card about interest compounding monthly, money earning money while you slept. It had struck him as almost symbiosis, the bank and the depositor each feeding the other, though he suspected the bank fed better. Two sides of the same principle, he thought: interest could grow what you kept or swell what you owed, and the only difference was which side of the counter you were standing on. He had planned, in a vague and probably profligate way, to blow his first paycheque on a better speaker. That plan now seemed like it belonged to a younger person.

"I have three hundred in my account at home," he said. "Well, I will have, once I deposit this." He lifted the envelope with his garden-centre cheque in it. "You can have two hundred. You pay me back twenty a week, no interest, and if you're late I'll just be sad at you quietly."

"You'd do that?"

"You held my shift when my grandmother died so I didn't lose the job. This is less than that." He stood up, and preempted her next argument, which he could see assembling itself behind her eyes, by walking to the counter and taking a numbered ticket from the dispenser. "Also I'm opening a savings account today, and I'd feel profligate doing it while you're sitting over there being miserable, so really this is for me."

She laughed then, really laughed, the sound bouncing off the marble, and the man at the pen island glanced over and smiled without looking up from his slip. When the teller called number forty-one, Elijah stepped forward, and Sarah came to stand beside him at the window, still holding her backpack but loosely now, one strap instead of both.

"Twenty a week," she said. "Starting Friday after next, not this one, this one's rent."

"Friday after next," he agreed, and slid his deposit slip and the envelope under the glass, and watched the teller stamp it with a small, official thump.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: The Hindu festival of Holi falls on the full moon of the month Phalguna, usually in March, and begins with a bonfire the night before called Holika Dahan.
story:
The bus from the city let Sara off at the end of her grandmother's lane just as the light was going amber over the fields. She had her admissions letter folded in the back pocket of her jeans, and a text from Hallie waiting on her phone, asking whether she was really going to spend her spring break at a farm with no signal instead of the dorm visit. Sara typed maybe both and put the phone away, because the lane was already crowded with relatives she half recognized, carrying armfuls of wood toward the open ground behind the house.

Her grandmother stood at the center of it all, directing uncles toward the pile with the flat certainty of a foreman. "It has to be tall," she was saying. "The taller the fire, the better the year." Sara kissed her cheek and was handed a bundle of twigs before she had said more than three words, which was how things were done here.

She had been eight the first time, the year her parents had sent her ahead of them on the train alone. In that memory the bonfire had seemed enormous, a pillar of heat she could feel through her winter coat, and the next morning her white kurta had turned a blue so deep it was almost a bruise. She had cried about the ruination of it, and her grandmother had laughed and said the cloth was better now, that the stain was a kind of blessing, and Sara had believed her completely, the way you can only believe something at eight.

Tonight she watched the wood stack up and found herself doing arithmetic against her will. The festival fell on the full moon of the month Phalguna, usually in March; her astronomy professor had drilled lunar phases into them all semester with a flashlight and a Styrofoam ball. She looked up and there it was, the moon a day from full, and something in her chest loosened at how the two calendars agreed with each other, the sacred one and the one on her syllabus. It was a coincidence of method rather than meaning, she told herself, and then wondered why she needed to tell herself anything at all.

Her cousin found her at the edge of the gathering, a taciturn boy of about fourteen who generally spoke only to ask for a charger. Tonight, though, he was full of ceremony. "It starts tonight," he said, nodding at the pile. "Holika Dahan. Tomorrow is the colors." He said it in the tone of someone reporting a score, but she caught the pride underneath it, and it made her fond of him in a way she had not been since he was small enough to boss around.

The uncles circled the wood with torches while the grandmother murmured the old prayers, and Sara stood with her hands in her pockets, caught between two ways of standing in front of a fire. One way was Hallie's way, the way of the seminar table: a combustion reaction, energy released, a human custom of externalizing the wish to burn away the old year because wishes have to go somewhere. The other way was her grandmother's, which needed no translation and made the translation feel slightly cheap. The fire caught all at once, with a sound like a held breath being let go, and the crowd moved inward, faces going gold.

"It's the full moon tomorrow," her grandmother said beside her, unexpected. "Phalguna. That's how we know when." Sara looked at her, this woman who had left school at eleven, who read the sky more reliably than the physics department read a calendar. There was no conflict in her, so far as Sara could see, between the moon as rock and the moon as clock. Perhaps the conflict had only ever been Sara's, a thing she carried like an argument she was having with no one.

The fire burned down and the family began drifting back toward the house, arguing happily about who would wake earliest for the colors. Sara stayed a minute longer, soot in her nose, warmth on one side of her face and the cold of the March night on the other. In the morning there would be pigment under her fingernails and in her hair, and in August there would be a dormitory and a Styrofoam ball and a city that ran on other people's schedules. She did not know yet how she would stand in both places without splitting.

She took out her phone, held it up toward the smoldering pile, and took a photograph for Hallie. Then she wrote, tell you tomorrow, and followed the lamplight into the house.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: A food bank is usually a central warehouse that collects and distributes food to local agencies, while a food pantry is where people pick up food directly.
story:
The warehouse smelled of cardboard and cold concrete, and Daniel had been there for two hours before he admitted to himself that something was wrong. He and Davin had signed up together, expecting a line of hungry people, gratitude, something visible. Instead they sorted dented cans into crates and wheeled pallets toward a loading dock where a van with a church logo waited. Nobody came for groceries. Nobody came in at all except drivers with clipboards.

"Maybe it's a slow day," Davin said, stacking soup. Daniel said nothing, but the thought gnawed at him, that they had been sent to the wrong room of the world, that the actual hunger was happening somewhere else, behind a door he hadn't found. He had wanted this volunteer day to be straightforward. His mother had pushed for it, framing it as penance for a semester of skipped homework, and he had agreed partly out of guilt and partly out of a vague idea that suffering, witnessed up close, would ionize him somehow, charge him into a better person. So far he mostly felt useful in the way a conveyor belt is useful.

Fanny arrived at noon, breathless, an hour late because she'd gone to the address on the flyer and found a small storefront with a queue outside it, then walked twenty minutes to the warehouse address printed in smaller font. "There were people there," she said. "A whole line. I thought that's where we were supposed to be." Daniel stopped mid-motion with a crate of rice in his hands.

Mr. Robinson, the coordinator, a wide man with a lanyard and a permanent half-smile, overheard and drifted over. "That's the pantry," he said. "We're the food bank."

Fanny looked blank. Daniel waited for more, but Mr. Robinson had already turned to shout at a driver about a pallet of oranges. So Daniel carried the crate to its place and turned the sentence over while he worked. The food bank. The pantry. The vans. The church logo, the school logo, the logo he didn't recognize. Things began to arrange themselves in his mind the way the crates arranged themselves on the shelf, and he felt the small private click of understanding: a food bank is usually a central warehouse that collects and distributes food to local agencies, while a food pantry is where people pick up food directly. The line Fanny had seen was the end of a chain that passed through this room, through his hands, through this afternoon.

He was still assembling this, feeling both pleased and slightly deflated by it, when the door at the front opened and a woman came in. She was young, younger than his mother, holding a toddler on one hip, and she stood in the aisle between pallets looking lost, the way a person looks when they've walked further than they meant to. The warehouse went quiet in a way that made the quiet noticeable. Davin set down his soup can very slowly.

"I'm sorry," she said. "They said, at the church, that there was food here. But the church is closed on Fridays now and we don't have anything in the house, and the baby." She stopped. The toddler grabbed a strand of her hair and pulled it, and she let him.

Daniel's understanding, so tidy a minute ago, turned equivocal. He knew now what the building was and was not. He knew the system moved food from here to agencies and that agencies handed it to people, and he knew that this woman was standing in the wrong building, and that telling her so felt like telling her the truth and like telling her nothing at all. Mr. Robinson was halfway across the warehouse and moving unhurriedly. The woman's eyes went from Daniel to the crates of sorted cans, to the pallets, to the door she'd come through, calculating, the way Daniel was calculating, whether walking back those blocks was possible before the pantry closed at four.

He glanced at Davin, who shrugged with his whole body, meaning I don't know, meaning your call. It occurred to Daniel that the whole afternoon had been a kind of asceticism without the point of asceticism, effort purified of contact, and that the contact was standing three feet away with wet eyes and a toddler chewing on her collar.

"There's a pantry," Daniel said, "about fifteen minutes from here, on Halstead. But listen, it closes at four." He pulled out his phone and checked the time, then held it up so she could see it. "It's twenty past three. If you want, I can call them and ask them to wait."

"You'd do that?"

He was already dialing, one hand pressed to his ear, watching her shift the toddler to the other hip.

activity: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
knowledge_domain: how income tax, sales tax and deductions show up on paycheques, receipts and tax returns
fact: US employers must generally give each employee a Form W-2 by the end of January, showing the previous year's wages and the taxes withheld, which is needed to file a tax return.
story:
The accountant's office smelled of toner and old paper, and Wyatt sat with his knees against a filing cabinet because the waiting area only had two chairs and an older man had taken one. On the wall behind the reception desk hung a framed certificate and, beside it, a poster that itemized nothing, just a sunrise and the words "Tax season ends April 15." He had taped his last paystub inside his folder, and beside it the receipts from the hardware store where he'd worked since June, though he could not have said exactly why he'd brought the receipts. The paystub was the thing. At the bottom, in a column smaller than the rest, it read Federal Income Tax Withheld, and the number next to it was $412, which was more money than he had ever voluntarily handed to anyone.

Ms. Desir came out at ten past four, reading a file as she walked. She was the neighbour who had offered to look at his paperwork before he filed for the first time, back when his mother mentioned at the mailbox that Wyatt had a job now. "You're the one with the summer job," she said, not a question, and she led him past the copy machine into a small room with two chairs and a window facing the parking lot.

He showed her the paystub first. She turned it over once, then set it down. "This is useful," she said, "but it isn't the document you file from. Your employer has to send you a Form W-2. It shows your wages for the whole previous year and the taxes that were withheld, and you need it to file your return." Wyatt said he'd heard something about a form, and she nodded. "By the end of January. If it's February and nothing's come, you call them."

It was April 8. He hadn't called anyone. He had assumed, in the way he assumed most administrative things would arrange themselves, that the money had gone where money goes and that the rest was a formality for other people. Ms. Desir did not look at him with pity, which was somehow worse, because pity he could have argued with.

She asked what he had. He laid out the receipts, and she picked up the longest one, from August, when he'd bought steel-toed boots because the foreman insisted. The receipt ran through the items, then added a line near the bottom: state sales tax, a few dollars on top of the price. "You pay that every time," she said, tapping the line, "though it's the store that sends it in. Different thing from income tax, which your employer takes out of your pay before you ever see it." Wyatt looked at the boot receipt again, at the two taxes sitting on the same slip of paper, one visible and one hidden, and something about that arrangement struck him as worth being suspicious of, though he couldn't articulate why.

"Are the boots a deduction?" he asked. He'd heard the word from Hayley, who had announced at lunch in March that her father's deductions were "basically free money." Hayley spoke about money the way she spoke about most things, with enormous confidence and partial information, and her scathing review of anyone who filed late had made him afraid to admit he hadn't filed at all.

Ms. Desir demurred, tilting her hand in the air. "That depends on things we won't know until we look," she said. "Deductions reduce what gets taxed. Whether yours qualify is a separate question." She pulled a blank worksheet toward her and began writing numbers in the margins while asking him questions: how much he'd made in total, whether he'd had another job, whether anyone could claim him as a dependent. He answered, and each answer became a number, and the numbers began to resemble a portrait of his year, sketched in ink.

His phone buzzed against his thigh. A message from Raphaelle, who had finished her own return in February and had been gentle about it, which he appreciated more than Hayley's competence. "Did you find the form? My mom's boyfriend says if the employer never sent it, you can still file, but it's more work. Call them tomorrow, first thing. April 15 doesn't move." He read it twice, then set the phone face-down on his knee. Tomorrow, first thing. The hardware store opened at seven.

The problem, as he understood it now, sitting in the small room while Ms. Desir drew arrows between columns, was that he'd been treating money as one thing when it was at least three. The wages on his stub were not the wages in his hand, because income tax had already left; the price on the boots was not the price he'd paid, because sales tax had been added at the register; and the taxes he'd already paid were not necessarily the taxes he owed, which was the whole reason for the return, the whole reason a form showing the year's wages and withheld taxes mattered in the first place. It was possible he'd paid too much. Hayley insisted everyone like him got money back, but Hayley also insisted that deductions were free money, and he no longer fully trusted either claim.

Ms. Desir stopped writing and looked at him. "You can call them tonight," she said. "The manager's probably still there." She wrote a number on a sticky note and slid it across the desk, and beneath the number she wrote "ask for the W-2" and underlined it once.

He stood in the parking lot with the folder under his arm and the note in his hand, and he thought, briefly and without any real conviction, that there was something almost existentialist about it, about a person assembling a self out of receipts and withheld wages and having to declare it to the government by a date certain. Then he dialled. A man answered on the third ring, said hold on, and Wyatt heard the phone being set down on a counter, keys jangling somewhere beyond it, a radio playing low. He waited, watching the light go flat and gold over the parked cars, and when the man came back he said, "Sorry, kid. What was it you needed?"

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: US inflation peaked at 14.8 percent in March 1980 and fell below 3 percent by 1983, after the Federal Reserve's sharp interest rate increases.
story:
The lemonade stand sat at the end of Hudson's driveway under a beach umbrella that had lost half its ribs, and by two o'clock it had earned four dollars and a handful of dimes. Sienna had come over supposedly to study, but she'd dragged the card table into the shade, set the pitcher between them, and opened the econ workbook anyway, so the two projects had merged into one afternoon. Her pencil tapped the page. "Question five. It gives you the graph and says explain the steep drop in the early eighties. You wrote one sentence and it's not even a sentence, it's a fragment with a period after it."

Hudson poured himself a glass he hadn't paid for. He knew the graph. Inflation climbing for years, then the line tipping over like a wave breaking, then falling hard through 1981 and 1982 before flattening near the bottom of the chart. He'd written that it "went down" and stopped, because he could see that it went down and could not, in any honest way, say why. Mr. Alvarez had circled the fragment twice in red and written, in the margin, the word that had been sitting in his stomach since Tuesday. Explain.

"So walk me through it," Sienna said. "You're the one who has to present it Monday. If you desensitize me to your terrible explanations now, the actual thing can only be an improvement." She was smiling, but she also wanted the stand to work, and she checked the street the way she'd been checking it all hour, watching for cars that never became customers. She needed thirty dollars by Friday for the concert ticket, and the four-dollar till was a quiet indictment of their pricing, their location, their signage, possibly their lemonade.

"Okay," Hudson said, and turned the notebook so she could see the graph. "Inflation peaked at fourteen point eight percent in March of 1980. Then it fell below three percent by 1983. That's the drop. That's what the question is about." He said it flat, the way he'd memorized it off the chart's caption, and Sienna nodded slowly, waiting, because that was the part anyone could read off the page.

"And?" she said. "Why? What happened?"

"The Federal Reserve raised interest rates. Sharply." He'd found that much in the textbook's index, chased it through two chapters, and it was true the way a photograph of a locked door was true. It showed him the door and nothing about the key. He pushed the pitcher toward a pickup truck that slowed, then didn't stop, then was gone. "Rates go up, and three years later inflation's under three percent. That's what happened. The book doesn't really say the in-between part."

Sienna frowned at the graph as if it were a person withholding something. "So say the in-between part yourself. You're allowed to think, it's not cheating." She tore a corner off the napkin stack, customers or no customers, and started folding it into something smaller and smaller. "If rates go up, what does that do?"

Hudson looked down the street, which was empty and shimmering, and made himself say it out loud, even the clumsy version. "Borrowing costs more. So people borrow less. And spend less. If everybody's spending less, prices stop climbing so fast." He heard it in his own voice and it sounded thin, a chain with the middle links missing, and he said so. "I don't know that that's the whole answer. I don't know how much pain it took, or how long, or what it cost people while the line was coming down. The graph doesn't show that part. It just shows it worked."

Before Sienna could answer, a car did stop, an actual car, and out of it came Mr. Chan from three doors down, a choleric man on trash day but patient at a lemonade stand, holding a thermos the size of a small child. "You're the economists," he said. "I saw the sign from the curb. Though your sign says lemonade and your table says homework, so I wasn't certain what you were selling." He studied their poster, which read FRESH LEMONADE $1 in Sienna's bubble letters, and then the pitcher, and then he said, "I'll take two glasses now, and I'll give you five dollars for the rest of that pitcher if you fill this."

Sienna had the thermos uncapped before he finished the sentence. While she poured, Mr. Chan drank one glass standing up and told them the sugar was right, that most people were afraid of the sugar, that this was a coward's economy in every direction. Hudson counted the money after the car pulled away: thirteen dollars, and their pitcher was empty, and they'd have to squeeze more lemons if anyone else came.

He put the bills in the tin and didn't hand Sienna her half right away. "Can I keep the till till tonight?" he said. "Dad's been out of work since March. I've been putting whatever this makes toward groceries and not saying anything, because it felt like saying it made it more real." He counted out her six dollars and set it on the table in front of her, separate from the rest, and she looked at it and then at the empty pitcher and started rolling up her sleeves.

"We can get maybe two more pitchers out of the bag in the kitchen," she said. "You bring the lemons, I'll redo the sign. People can't read bubble letters from a moving car." She was already up and moving toward the garage door, marker in hand.

activity: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
knowledge_domain: to trace the steps of cellular respiration from glucose to ATP in the mitochondria
fact: The citric acid cycle turns twice for each glucose molecule, because one glucose produces two acetyl-CoA molecules and each enters the cycle separately.
story:
Florence had commandeer of the picnic table before anyone else claimed it, which meant spreading her poster board across both benches and weighting the corners with her mother's river stones. On the poster she had drawn the whole route in marker: glucose at the top like a departing train, glycolysis splitting it in half, then the long descent into the mitochondria where the citric acid cycle waited in a loop she had colored red. Talia arrived first, carrying a bag of clementines, and sat down without asking whether she was welcome.

"Ms. Sato said our tallies have to balance," Florence said. "Mine don't. I'm off by almost half, and I've checked the arrows four times."

Talia peeled a clementine and offered half of it across the table. She was supposed to be studying for a driving test, not this, and everyone in the study group knew it, but she had come anyway because Florence had texted three times and then once more with a photograph of the poster looking wounded. Talia's own want sat quietly beside her: a license before Labor Day, an escape route from asking her father for rides. Still, she picked up a marker and said, "Show me where it goes wrong."

Florence traced the path with her finger, narrating under her breath. Glucose enters, gets broken in glycolysis, becomes two smaller pieces, and those pieces become something called acetyl-CoA, which drops into the cycle. She had written the cycle's yield once, in careful numerals beside the red loop, and then carried those numbers down to the final ATP total. The total was wrong.
