She had known it was wrong since Tuesday, and the wrongness had settled over the week like a kind of ennui, a gray film over even the parts she understood.

Maximus came through the back gate eating a popsicle he had clearly taken from Florence's freezer without asking, which was its own long-standing arrangement between them. He leaned over the poster, dripping slightly, and Talia moved the clementines out of range. "Your loop," he said, tapping the red circle. "How many times does it spin per glucose?"

"Once," Florence said. "One glucose, one turn. That's how I counted it." She said it with more confidence than she felt, and Maximus gave her a look that was noncommittal in the way he used when he suspected she was wrong but wanted her to find it herself, which she both appreciated and resented.

She stared at the poster. She followed her own arrows again, slower this time. Glycolysis had split the glucose into two pieces, and each of those pieces became an acetyl-CoA, and each one entered the cycle separately, which meant the loop did not spin once, it spun twice. "The citric acid cycle turns twice for each glucose molecule," she said, half to the poster and half to the two of them. "Because one glucose produces two acetyl-CoA molecules, and each enters the cycle separately." She sat back. "Everything after glycolysis happens twice. Everything I tallied once."

Talia, who had been holding the marker without using it, pulled the poster toward her and began adding a small numeral two beside the red loop. "So you have to double all of this," she said, circling the region below the split. It was the most biochemistry Talia had voluntarily performed in her life, and when Florence looked up, surprised, Talia shrugged. "You checked my parallel parking diagram for an hour last month. Turnabout." She kept circling. "Also I'm not leaving until your numbers balance, so hurry up."

They worked through the arithmetic together while Maximus narrated the glucose's journey in the voice of a travel announcer, which helped no one but made Talia laugh so hard she had to put the marker down. When the totals finally matched, at the bottom of the poster in Florence's handwriting, Ms. Sato's promised balance restored, Florence took the last clementine segment Talia had saved for her and placed it ceremonially on the mitochondria.

"For the cycle," she said. "It earned it."

activity: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
knowledge_domain: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
fact: Affirming the consequent is a logical fallacy: from 'if P then Q' and 'Q', concluding 'P'. Living in San Diego means living in California, but living in California does not mean living in San Diego.
story:
Anna found the study room first, the one with the window facing the parking lot, and spread her debate materials across the table before anyone else could claim it. The state qualifiers were in nine days. Her case argued that the city should fund early childhood education, and she knew the evidence cold, which was exactly the problem, because Darius kept beating her anyway.

He arrived with Alivia, both of them carrying coffees they weren't supposed to have in the library, and Darius set his cup down on her stack of research like a flag planted in territory. "Same drill," he said. "I'm the opposition. You open."

She opened. She gave the study, the sample size, the effect on reading scores. Darius nodded along, waited, then said, "Cities with strong pre-K programs vote for school funding. Your city has a school funding problem. So your city lacks pre-K." He paused. "That's your case, Anna. Flipped."

"That's not my case."

"It's your shape, though." He tapped the paper. "You keep doing this. You show that good outcomes showed up after the policy, and you act like the policy caused them. Maybe rich cities do both. Maybe parents who'd enroll their kids were already reading to them at night."

Alivia, who had been drawing mountains in her notebook, looked up. "There's a name for that," she said. "We did it in logic. Affirming the consequent. If it rained the lawn is wet, the lawn is wet, so it rained. Except the sprinkler."

Anna stared at her. "The sprinkler?"

"The lawn is wet for some other reason. San Diego's in California, but living in California doesn't mean you live in San Diego." Alivia went back to her mountains. "Darius read that chapter too. He's been farming you all season."

The word resuscitate was floating through Anna's head because her coach had used it last week, told her the case needed resuscitating, and she'd bristled at it, the way you bristle when someone implies the patient was already dying. She looked down at her cards and saw it plainly: three of her four contentions had the same hole. If pre-K then reading gains. Reading gains present. Therefore pre-K. She'd never once checked for sprinklers.

"Again," she said. "Same argument. I'll fix it live."

Ms. Charles, the librarian, knocked twice on the glass and pointed at the coffees. Darius moved his off the research with exaggerated care. When she'd gone, he turned bellicose, which for Darius meant he leaned forward and dropped the friendly tone entirely. "You can't fix it live. The flaw is in the design, not the delivery."

"Then redesign it."

"Fine. What's your strongest card?"

She chose the twins study, the one where the kids who attended and the kids who didn't were matched on everything measurable. "Same families, same neighborhoods, same parents' education," she said. "The differences that showed up, they showed up after the program. And the kids who didn't attend, they matched on the stuff that would've been my sprinkler."

"Matched on everything measurable," Alivia said, not looking up. "Measurable is doing a lot of work in that sentence."

"That's the honest version," Anna said, and the sentence surprised her as she said it. "I can't prove it was the program and only the program. I can prove the obvious other explanations were checked for. If someone's going to beat me, they have to find a sprinkler nobody measured."

Darius sat back. He rolled the coffee cup between his palms, the way he did when he was deciding whether an opponent had actually improved or had just said something that sounded like improvement. "Say the conditional out loud," he said. "The real one, not the one you want."

"If pre-K, then gains, all else equal."

"And?"

"And all else wasn't equal in my other cards, so they're out. This one card, plus a framework that says we should act under uncertainty when the cost of being wrong is small and the cost of ignoring it is large." She stacked the three dead contentions, squared them, and set them at the edge of the table like something for the return cart. "I'm not going to claim more than the study claims."

Alivia ripped a page from her notebook and slid it across. She'd written two columns: Things Anna Can Prove, and Things Anna Believes Anyway. The second column was longer. "You still have to argue from somewhere," Alivia said. "Just know which column you're in."

Ms. Charles appeared at the door again, this time holding a flyer for a logic workshop on Thursday evenings, and set it on the table without a word before walking away. Anna picked it up. Thursday. Nine days minus qualifiers left almost nothing, but the Thursday before was empty, and she could see from the flyer that the second session covered fallacies, which meant everyone else at qualifiers would have Alivia's chapter, which meant her advantage would last exactly one round.

She looked at Darius. "You knew the whole time. The sprinkler thing. You've known since September."

He shrugged. "It's not my job to teach the opposition."

"Then why tell me now?"

He stood, gathered his coat, and drained the last of the contraband coffee. "Because I heard the state finals don't have a second seed," he said. "If we both get there, I want it to be because your best case lost to my best case. Not because you never found your sprinkler." He nodded at the flyer in her hand. "Thursday. I'll save you a seat."

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
knowledge_domain: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
fact: Doubling the size of a sorted list adds only one extra step to a binary search, while it doubles the worst-case work of a linear search.
story:
The porch boards at his grandfather's house had been painted so many times that the knots in the wood had become small impermeable bumps, and Cameron ran his thumb over one while the laptop booted. Rylan sat across from him with his own machine open, and between them lay the robotics team's parts list, exported that morning to a spreadsheet: four hundred rows, where yesterday there had been two hundred. Brooklyn had texted them both at six a.m. Somebody's inventory merge had gone wrong, or right, depending on how you counted, and now every lookup their robot ran during the demo would be tested against double the data.

"It's fine," Rylan said. "Lookups are fast. That's the whole point of a computer."

"Yesterday it wasn't fast. Remember the stall at the edge of the practice field?" Cameron opened the two functions they'd written the week before. One of them, the one Rylan had written, walked the list from the top, row by row, comparing the part number until it matched. The other, Cameron's, jumped to the middle of the sorted list, decided which half the target had to be in, and threw the other half away. "Yours is a linear search," Cameron said. "Mine's a binary search. Try yours on the new list."

Rylan's fingers went quiet on the keys. He ran the lookup, then ran it a hundred times in a loop, the way Ms. De Vries had taught them in the spring, timing each pass with the counter she'd insisted they build into everything. Then he leaned back and read the number twice. "It's about double. The whole run took about twice as long as it did on the two-hundred-row list."

"Now run mine." Cameron watched his friend's face while the loop finished, because the number was going to land before any explanation did. It had taken Cameron three evenings to get the function working at all; the first version had an off-by-one error that made it miss every part sitting exactly at a boundary, and Ms. De Vries had refused to fix it for him, only asking, each Monday, whether he had tested the edges. He had, eventually, hated it, and then fixed it.

"One extra step," Rylan said slowly, scrolling the counter. "The two-hundred list took eight steps in the worst case. The four-hundred list takes nine. We doubled everything and you gained one step, and I doubled my whole workload." He looked up, and something in his expression had shifted from defensiveness to curiosity, which Cameron had learned was the better half of Rylan. "Okay. That's the demo saved. But don't pathologize my code, all right? The linear one isn't sick, it's just doing the honest thing in order."

"The honest thing in order is going to get us laughed off the field," Cameron said, but he said it while sliding the last of the coffee cake across the table, because Rylan had been up since five and had eaten nothing. There was a subtlety to Rylan that people at school missed, mostly because he talked so much: he gave away his best ideas to anyone who seemed stuck, and remembered, months later, which ones he'd given. Cameron had built his whole understanding of searching on a diagram Rylan had doodled on a napkin in September, before either of them knew the word for it. Which meant, he thought, that the credit on this belonged somewhere murkier than either of their names, and he didn't entirely know where.

From the doorway, Brooklyn had been watching the two of them for a while before either noticed. She had her phone in her hand with the screen dark, and her expression had the careful impermeability she wore when she'd decided not to say something. Rylan saw it first. He had known her since seventh grade and could read her silences the way Cameron read code.

"Brooklyn." He nudged the chair beside him out with his foot. "Sit down. It's fixed, mostly. Cameron's function barely noticed the new list, and mine fell over, and we're going to swap mine out before the demo. But that's not what you came to say."

She sat, and turned the phone over, and turned it back. "My dad's coming to the demo," she said. "He's never come to anything." She looked at the spreadsheet, at the four hundred rows, and then at Cameron's function on the screen, still holding its nine steps. "He thinks robotics is a hobby for kids who can't do real math. I wanted the demo to be fast so he'd just see it working and not ask how."

Cameron closed the laptop halfway, the way you do when a conversation stops being about the screen. "Or," Rylan said, "we show him the slow one and the fast one side by side, and you tell him why doubling the data only cost you one extra step. Make him ask how."

Brooklyn didn't answer, but she pulled the laptop back open toward herself, and scrolled up to the counter, and read the number again.

activity: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
knowledge_domain: ethical questions raised by technology such as algorithmic bias, surveillance and automation
fact: A 2013 study by Carl Benedikt Frey and Michael Osborne estimated that 47 percent of US jobs were at high risk of automation.
story:
The kiosk arrived at the coffee shop on a Tuesday, bolted to the counter beside the register like a patient waiting to be seen. Rebecca had worked the morning shift for eleven months by then, long enough to know that Mr. Munro, the retired engineer from the corner house, ordered a large drip with room for cream at 7:40 sharp, and that the machine was the manager's answer to the afternoon rush she couldn't cover alone. She wiped down the steam wand and watched the installer fish cables through a hole he'd drilled in the laminate.

"They say it learns," Abbigail said, sliding onto a stool with her backpack still on one shoulder. She was between classes at the community college, and she said everything lately as though she had read it somewhere, which she usually had. "It remembers what people order. It suggests a muffin."

"It suggests a muffin because a muffin has the highest margin," Rebecca said. "That's not learning. That's arithmetic wearing a nicer shirt." She said it lightly, but she had spent part of her break the night before reading the manufacturer's page on her phone, hunched in the back room among the coffee-stained rags, curious in spite of herself about what the thing actually did. It counted. It sorted. It flagged orders that looked unusual.

Mr. Munro came in at 7:40 and studied the kiosk the way he studied crossword clues, with polite suspicion. "You'll be out of a job by Christmas, then," he said, and Abbigail, who had been waiting all morning for a hook, told him about a paper she'd cited for an essay. "A 2013 study by Carl Benedikt Frey and Michael Osborne estimated that 47 percent of US jobs were at high risk of automation." She recited it perfectly, the way she recited everything, and Mr. Munro nodded as though she had reported the weather.

Rebecca poured his cream and did not say anything right away, but later, when the morning thinned out, she looked the study up herself, sitting on the milk crate by the grinder. Forty-seven percent. She tried to place herself inside that number and couldn't decide where she fell. The kiosk could take an order. It could not carry a tray to the woman with the stroller, or notice that the boy from the high school was buying a large hot chocolate every single day and had stopped meeting anyone's eyes. She had noticed that in September and had started drawing a small dog on his cup, badly, and he had started drawing them back on the napkins.

But she was honest enough with herself to see the other side of it, and she turned both ideas over the way she cogitated over essay prompts, slowly, letting each one have its turn. The machine never shorted the drawer. It never called in sick during finals week. And there was something in her that bristled at being doctrinaire about it, at declaring the kiosk evil from a stool, the way Abbigail sometimes declared things, whole industries condemned in a single sentence. Abbigail had a chronology for everything, a tidy sequence of causes and effects that ended wherever her argument needed it to end. Rebecca's own thinking kept refusing to line up that neatly. The machine was convenient and it was a threat and it was also, she had to admit, faintly fascinating, and all three of those could be true at once.

By Friday the kiosk was live, and the afternoon rush proved stranger than anyone predicted. Half the customers used it without being asked. The other half walked past it deliberately, stood in Rebecca's line, and looked at her with a defiant tenderness she hadn't asked for, as though buying a latte from a person had become a small act of resistance. The boy with the hot chocolate chose the machine. She watched his order appear on her screen, itemized and prepaid, and watched him wait at the end of the counter with nothing to draw on. She drew the dog anyway, on the cup, before she made it, and when she handed it over he looked at it for a long second and then at her.

At closing the manager came by with numbers on his phone. The kiosk had handled more orders per hour than Rebecca, and the afternoon receipts were up, and he said this in the bright voice of a man delivering good news to a room where nobody had asked for it. He also said, almost as an aside, that his payroll budget was now thirty hours a week instead of forty, effective the first of the month, and that she should think about which shifts mattered most to her. Rebecca nodded and stacked the chairs. She was still working out what she thought, exactly, both sides of it turning in her like milk in a pitcher, neither one winning. Outside the window, under the streetlight, the boy from the high school was sitting on the bench with his cup, drawing something on a napkin after all.

She went out to see, hands still warm from the steam wand. He held the napkin up to the light so she could read it. It said, in careful block letters, THANK YOU MACHINE GIRL.

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
knowledge_domain: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
fact: On many ocean current maps, warm currents are drawn with red arrows and cold currents with blue arrows.
story:
I have always been good at maps, which is why Mr. Doyle asked me to run the ocean current table at the museum's volunteer day instead of grading worksheets in the back room like Ziyad and Karis. That is my account of it, anyway, and I have repeated it enough times that it feels like the true one. In fact Mr. Doyle asked all three of us, and I volunteered myself for the map before anyone else could speak, which is a slightly different thing.

The table sat under the big blue dome of the ocean hall, beside a tank of quiescent jellyfish that pulsed once every few seconds, as if breathing for something else. A laminated map of the North Atlantic was taped to the table's edge. Arrows crawled across it in two colors, red and blue, and I had looked at it for perhaps a minute before the first family arrived, which I later described to Karis as "long enough to master it."

The family had a boy of about ten who pressed his finger to a red arrow crawling up the western edge of the map, past the tip of Florida and on toward the pale smear of Britain. "That one's the fastest," the boy said. "Red means fast. Like in racing."

I almost said yes. I wanted to say yes, because I had decided, in my minute of mastery, that the red arrows were the important ones, the powerful ones, and powerful meant fast, and fast meant red, and the loop of reasoning closed so neatly that it felt like knowledge. Then Ziyad drifted over from the worksheet table, looked at the map over the boy's shoulder, and ruined everything.

"No, it's not speed," Ziyad said. "Warm currents are drawn with red arrows and cold currents are blue. That's the convention." He said it flatly, the way he said most things, and tapped the blue arrow running down the eastern edge, the one I had barely glanced at because it was heading the wrong way, south, away from anything I cared about. "So this cold one flows down from the Arctic, and that red one flows north."

I felt the urge to excoriate him, honestly I did, to point out that I had been about to say something adjacent, that we were in agreement, that the difference was trivial. But it wasn't trivial. The boy was looking at me, waiting to see which adult-shaped person to believe, and I had nothing. I said, "Ziyad's right," and hated the smallness of the sentence, and then knelt down next to the boy, because kneeling buys time and also changes the angle of the conversation.

"Look," I said, tracing the red arrow north with my finger, away from the warm Caribbean water, up along the coast, out across the whole gray Atlantic toward Ireland and Norway. "It carries warm water a long way north. Warm water, red arrow. Same rule on every map like this one." I stopped there, because that was as far as I actually knew. The map showed the red line reaching Europe; whether warmth traveled with it, whether the little houses in the pictures of Norwegian fjords owed anything to this particular drawn line, I could not say, and I found that the honesty of that was almost pleasant, once I stopped trying to hide it.

Karis arrived with the worksheets in time to hear me say "I don't know" to the boy's next question, which was whether the blue arrows meant the water was slow. She raised an eyebrow at me. "Felix admitting uncertainty. Should I be recording this?"

"You could be less delighted about it," I said, and she laughed and sat down on the table's edge, and the boy, who had lost interest in our disputes, drew his finger along the red arrow again, slowly, from the hot colors at the bottom of the map all the way to the cold ones at the top, murmuring the route to himself. Later I would tell people I taught him how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe, and I would nearly believe it. What actually happened is that Ziyad knew the colors, I knew the geography, and the boy made the connection himself, out loud, in his own crooked ten-year-old vocabulary, while I knelt there holding the map flat against the table with both hands.

Mr. Doyle came by at closing to collect the laminates. He looked at the map, then at me. "Anything you couldn't answer today?"

"One thing," I said. "Whether knowing which way the arrows point counts as understanding them."

He considered that longer than I expected, then rolled up the map and tucked it under his arm. "Ask me again in four years," he said, and walked off toward the jellyfish tank, where the water had finally gone still.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Research by linguist Paul Nation and colleagues suggests readers need to know about 98 percent of the words in a text to understand it comfortably without help.
story:
I'm good at languages, is the thing. I told everyone that in June, when Ms. McKenzie assigned us a short news article in a language we'd never studied, plus a spoken summary in September. I picked Portuguese because my grandmother spoke it, though she died before I was born, which I admitted to no one, since it sounded like the beginning of a novel and I wanted it to sound like a genealogy instead: language passed down, blood asserting itself. On the first night I opened an article about a change in the Brazilian tax code, because it looked serious, and I understood eleven words in the first paragraph. I told myself it was going well anyway. That's the part I have to be honest about: for three weeks I circled words in yellow highlighter and called that progress, and when my mother asked how it was going I said, nonchalant, "Easy," and went back upstairs to be confused in private.

The article refused to become easy. Every sentence was a locked box with one hinge visible. I copied vocabulary into a notebook until the notebook looked like a ledger of everything I didn't know, and I began to suspect the problem wasn't me, which was a strange relief and a humiliation at once.

Then Emie called, mid-July, from her kitchen where she was babysitting a younger brother who kept yelling about a video game. She had picked Greek. "How many words do you actually know on your page?" she asked, chewing something. "Like, out of a hundred. Count." I counted a random paragraph. Nineteen. "I'm at about thirty," she said. "And I found this thing last night. A linguist, Paul Nation, did research on it with other people. Readers need to know about 98 percent of the words in a text to understand it comfortably without help. Ninety-eight. Not fifty. Not seventy." She let that sit while her brother screamed about a goal. "So we're both reading the wrong articles."

From Emie's side of the call, the boy named Dominic went quiet for a long moment, and she could hear a chair scrape, then keyboard keys, then nothing. She almost hung up. When he came back his voice had changed, less performance in it. "I need an article where I know almost every word," he said, "which is impossible in a language I've never studied, unless." He stopped. She waited, the way she'd learned to wait with him, because he narrated his own competence and you had to let the narration run out before the real person appeared.

Unless the article was short, and about something so ordinary the vocabulary was tiny. I searched in English first: simple news, easy Portuguese. I found a three-paragraph piece about a historic bakery in Lisbon closing after ninety years, and I understood maybe seventy words of it on the first pass, which is not ninety-eight percent but is not nineteen either. I read it eleven times. I read it out loud to my bedroom wall, badly, and my mother knocked to ask if I was okay, and I said yes and meant it, which was new.

Here's where I have to stop trusting my own account, because I'd been telling myself a story all summer: chosen language, inherited gift, natural talent. The truth is I'd chosen an impossible text to prove something, and the proof I got was the opposite. But the bakery article let me hold two ideas at once, which felt like actual thinking. One: the difficulty had a shape, a number attached to it by researchers I'd never meet, and the number said nothing about my worth, only about my choice of text. Two: easy was not the same as cheating. Ms. McKenzie had asked for a summary, not a feat. A hard article poorly understood and a simple article honestly told were not the same work, and only one of them was a summary. What stayed uncertain was whether I could actually speak it aloud to a room, because reading alone and standing in front of twenty classmates are different animals, and no research I'd found had a percentage for that.

In August I practiced on Kamila, who was doing Mandarin and had independently found the same research, which made me like her more. She made me stand up in her driveway to do it, because sitting felt like hiding. "O pão era bom," I said, then in English, "the bread was good, the customers cried, the owner is eighty-one and tired." Kamila nodded once, the way she did at swim meets when a time was decent but not the point. "You summarized it," she said. "It happened. That's the assignment." I wanted to historicize the moment, place it at the start of some grand personal timeline, and I tried, and then I gave it up, because the driveway was hot and her little brother was spraying the hose at the pavement and the moment was just a moment, small and finished.

On the first Friday of school, Ms. McKenzie wrote her name on the board and said whoever wanted to go first should simply stand. The room smelled like floor wax and new binders. My summary took ninety seconds. My accent was wrong in at least four places, and a girl in the second row winced at one of them, kindly or not, I couldn't tell. When I sat down my hands were still shaking, and Kamila caught my eye across the room and raised one finger: one down, and there was a whole year left.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Food Banks Canada's HungerCount 2025 recorded nearly 2.2 million food bank visits in Canada in March 2025, a record for a single month.
story:
The community room of the residence smelled of floor wax and coffee, and by ten in the morning the line of folding chairs along the wall was already full. Maxime had been told to expect maybe twenty people. He counted forty-one before he stopped counting, and the food bank did not open for another half hour. Vicky, who had volunteered here since September, handed him a clipboard and a roll of stickers without looking up from her own list.

"You take names and household sizes," she said. "Most of them are residents, so it's fast. Some come in from outside, from the buses. Don't rush the ones who want to talk."

Mr. Rossi was third in line, though he lived two floors up and could have come down at noon. He wore a cardigan with a hole at the elbow and he watched Maxime work with the frank attention of a man who had nothing else scheduled. When Maxime reached him, the old man said, "New. I'd remember you. The other one had a beard."

"First day," Maxime said. "Household size?"

"One, unless you count the ficus." Rossi signed his name in a slow, deliberate hand. "You look like my nephew did before he learned to worry."

The outside people were the ones who took longer. A woman with two grandchildren counted them on her fingers as though the number might have changed since Tuesday. A man in a security uniform still warm from a night shift fell asleep in his chair and had to be shaken gently when the line moved. Maxime kept writing, and somewhere around the twentieth name he noticed that the arithmetic of the morning had stopped being numbers to him. The pile of grocery bags by the door, which had looked generous at nine, was visibly dwindling, and each tick on his clipboard was a bag that would not be there by one o'clock.

When there was a lull, Vicky showed him her phone. She had a page saved, some report she'd had to read for a class. "I found this last week and I still can't get over it," she said. "Food Banks Canada's HungerCount. The 2025 one. It recorded nearly 2.2 million food bank visits in Canada in March 2025. That's a record for a single month." She held the screen toward him as if the number needed a witness. "March. One month."

"Almost 2.2 million," Maxime said, because he had learned that precision mattered when the numbers were this size, though he heard how pedantic it sounded the moment it left his mouth.

"Fine, nearly 2.2 million," Vicky said. "Still. On a Tuesday. Look at this line. This is a Tuesday, Maxime."

He looked. Mrs. Okafor from the fourth floor was explaining to the man behind her how to stretch a bag of lentils across three dinners, and the man was writing it on the back of a receipt. Mr. Rossi had reached the table and was choosing his cans with the care of a man selecting wine, and Maxime realized that for the residents the line was not only want, it was also the day's event, the place where the building's loneliness got sorted into pairs and small groups. It was both things at once. He could not make those two things into one idea, and he suspected he wasn't supposed to.

The bags ran out at half past twelve. Vicky and Maxime stood at the emptied table while the last few people were apologized to and given slips for next week. Mr. Rossi lingered, helping stack the chairs, though nobody had asked him to.

"In my day we called this charity and kept our eyes down," he said. "Now you fill out a form and hold your head up. I haven't decided which is better. Probably both. Probably neither." He laughed a dry little laugh. "I keep coming back every week. My daughter calls it my recidivism. She thinks she's funny."

Maxime laughed too, and felt the laugh sit oddly beside the slip of paper in his shirt pocket, the one he'd taken from the leftover pile because he'd wanted, in some embryonic way he couldn't yet name, to keep a record of what forty-one households looked like on a Tuesday. The two ideas he'd carried in that morning, that volunteering was a favour he was doing and that it was a debt someone was paying, had not merged. They sat side by side, and he let them.

He carried the last chairs to the storage closet, and when he came back Mr. Rossi was gone, but on the table where the man had been sitting there was a can of peaches, set neatly aside from the rest, with a note in that slow deliberate hand: for the woman with the grandchildren, if she comes back.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: A 'best before' date marks when a food's quality may start to decline, not when it becomes unsafe, so sealed food past that date may still be safe to eat.
story:
The flyer had said community food bank, so Madison had pictured a church basement, and instead she found herself standing in a cinder-block room attached to the animal shelter on Greer Street, where the yipping of small dogs drifted through the shared wall like a metronome nobody had asked for. Ms. De Vries, who apparently ran both operations and moved between them in one pair of rubber boots, handed Madison a hairnet and a clipboard. "Sorting table's by the window," she said. "You'll be with Tyrese and Ophelie. They've done this four times, which makes them insufferable, but they're good."

Tyrese was already seated behind a mound of donated cans, holding one up to the light like a jeweler. Ophelie had claimed the marker and was labelling boxes with an enthusiasm that suggested the boxes had wronged her. "You're new," Tyrese said, not turning around. "Don't touch the parmesan. It's a long story." Madison sat down anyway, and the story, when it came, was prolix enough that she understood why he'd warned her: apparently a man named Gerald had donated eleven shakers of expired parmesan two Saturdays running, and the debate over their fate had outlasted the shift.

Today's problem was different. Madison pulled a can of peaches from the donation bag, checked the bottom, and frowned. The date stamped there was nine days past. She reached for the discard bin, the way the training sheet seemed to imply, and then stopped, because something about throwing away perfectly sealed peaches made her stomach fold in half. She turned the can over twice, as if a second reading might change the stamp.

"Wait," said Ophelie, leaning over. "Don't toss that yet."

"Why not? It's expired."

"It's not, though." Ophelie took the can and tapped the stamp with one chewed fingernail. "See, it says best before. That's not an expiry. A best before date is when the quality might start to decline, not when it becomes unsafe. Sealed food past that date can still be safe to eat." She said it fast and bored, like reciting a fire drill, and then went back to her boxes.

Madison looked at the peaches again. Somewhere behind the wall, a dog with a voice like a rusty hinge announced itself. "Then why does it feel like poison?" she asked.

"Because the stamp looks official," Tyrese said. "Dates have that power. They disenfranchise your brain. You see a number, you stop thinking, you just obey."

"That's a lot of philosophy for a can of peaches."

"I've been here four times. You get philosophy or you get parmesan stories. Pick your lane."

Madison laughed, then caught herself laughing, because the peaches mattered more than she'd first thought. If the can was still good, then the three cans beneath it were too, and the boxes at the end of the table, and possibly an entire shelf in the back that Ms. De Vries had marked with red tape. She carried the peaches over to where the older woman was wrestling a bag of kibble through the connecting door, a terrier escaping behind her like a punctuation mark. "Ms. De Vries, the red tape shelf. Is that all past date?"

"Best before," Ms. De Vries corrected, breathless, the terrier orbiting her ankles. "Why, what are you planning?"

"Nothing yet," Madison said, which was true, and also a small lie, because she was planning something and it was taking shape faster than she could examine it.

What she wanted, she realized as she sorted, was to be a person who did the right thing, but the right thing kept splitting in two like a road she hadn't been given a map for. On one side was caution: nobody at a food bank should ever get sick, and a mistake there landed on people who already had too much landing on them. On the other side was waste, a whole shelf of sealed food in a town where the same people stood in line every Wednesday. Her mother would have said better safe than sorry. Her economics teacher would have drawn a graph. Neither of them, Madison suspected, had ever held a can of nine-day-old peaches while a terrier barked at a mop bucket.

She went back to Ophelie. "Okay, so it can still be safe. Can. How do we know when it isn't?"

Ophelie set down her marker, which was itself an event. "That," she admitted, "is a way better question than you get credit for." Tyrese raised the peaches and studied them again, and for once said nothing, which between the three of them felt like a form of applause. They compromised: cans that were sealed and only recently past the date went into a separate box with a note, and anything bulging or dented or smelling like regret went out, and the note said plainly what the box was, so that the people choosing from it got to do the choosing.

Madison wrote the note herself, twice, because her first draft was prolix and her second was worse, and her third just said: past best before, still sealed, quality may have declined, safe to check. Tyrese read it over her shoulder and said, "'Safe to check' is basically an oxymoron, but a nice one," and Madison said it was not an oxymoron at all and he was thinking of a different word, and Ophelie ruled that they were both unbearable and confiscated the pen.

At the end of the shift, the red-tape shelf was half empty and the terrier had been adopted by a woman in a green coat, which everyone agreed was the plot twist of the day. Madison pulled off the hairnet and looked at the box she'd made, still not entirely sure it was the right box, still sure it was better than the bin. Ms. De Vries came through the connecting door with the smell of kibble and bleach trailing her and put one boot up on the sorting table. "Same time next week?" she said. "Gerald's been in again. There are shakers."

"How many?" Madison asked.

"Fourteen," said Ms. De Vries, and behind the wall, in what could only be interpreted as solidarity, every dog in the shelter began to howl.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: Most US employment is at-will, meaning the employer or the worker can end the job at any time for any reason that is not illegal.
story:
Amelia folded the application across the handlebars of her bike and pushed through the chain-link gate of the Marsten Aquatic Center at seven fifty in the morning, ten minutes before her interview. Ms. Haile, the aquatics director, met her at the front desk with a coffee-stained binder and a whistle already around her neck. "Certification current?" she asked, and Amelia produced the card from her back pocket, the laminate soft from sitting on it all June. The interview lasted eleven minutes. Most of it was Ms. Haile explaining that the outdoor pools opened Saturday, that every guard had to be on deck for opening day, and that Amelia, if she took the job, would start tomorrow with a shadow shift under a guard named Zaid.

Walking out, Amelia's phone buzzed. The day camp where she had really wanted to work, the one with the arts program and the lake and the other counselors her age, had finally called back. They wanted her, too. They needed an answer by Friday, and they started Monday, which meant she could not do both, because the pool required a season-long commitment through August and the camp ran the same weeks. She sat on the curb outside the aquatic center with her wetsuit still damp in her bag and felt the whole summer narrow to a single decision with a date stamped on it.

She took the pool job anyway, provisionally, telling herself she would figure something out. On Thursday she stood her first shadow shift at the deep well, and it was there that Zaid, who was loquacious in the way of people who have spent many hours alone on a tall chair, talked through the whole rotation while scanning the water. He was nineteen, had guarded three summers, and knew everyone. "Watch the kid in the red trunks," he said. "He dives where it's shallow." Then, apropos of nothing, because a man in lane four had been complaining loudly at the office about being bumped from his swim time: "Guy wants to sue. Thinks he owns the lane." Zaid snorted. "Job's at-will, so they could fire us tomorrow for no reason at all, any reason that isn't illegal, and we can quit the same way. Notice is a courtesy, not a law. I read the handbook cover to cover my first week."

Amelia blew her whistle at the kid in the red trunks before she answered, because she was already learning that the whistle came first. "So nobody has to give two weeks or anything?"

"Here they like it. Ms. Haile won't blacklist you if you're decent about it. But legally, no." He said it lightly, still scanning, and the fact settled into her the way water temperature does, not all at once.

That night she called Eloise, who had worked at the camp the previous summer and owed Amelia for covering her lab write-ups in the spring. "It's the best summer you'll ever have," Eloise said, and then, because she was honest even when it was inconvenient, "But they overbooked counselors last year and cut two of them in July. Mid-season. Just, here's your last paycheck, bye." Amelia lay on her bed turning that over. The pool could drop her the same way, she supposed; the freedom Zaid described ran in both directions, and the camp had already shown which direction it liked. She had wanted the camp for the feeling of it, the lake and the friends, and she had taken the pool for the money and the steady hours, and now she discovered she could actually choose, or quit, or be quit, at any time, for any reason that wasn't illegal, and no one would be breaking a law either way. That was either terrifying or freeing, and she could not decide which, and she had until Friday to decide something.

Friday morning she came to the pool early, before the recreation swimmers, when the water was flat and blue and so clean it seemed to exhilarate the air above it. She found Ms. Haile restocking the first-aid station and stood in the doorway holding the binder she had been given, her thumb on the page she had read four times. "I got another offer," Amelia said. "The camp. They need an answer today."

Ms. Haile did not stop counting gauze rolls. "And you want to take it."

"I don't know. Opening day is tomorrow. If I leave now you have to cover my chair, and everyone's shifts get longer, and the swimmers get a guard who's been on deck for six hours instead of four. It's not just me it lands on." She heard herself say it and recognized that she meant it, that she had actually been thinking about the rotation, about Zaid's day, about the kid in the red trunks.

Ms. Haile set down the gauze. "We'd manage. We always manage. But I'll tell you the same thing I tell every guard: the pool will forget you in a week. You won't forget what you did. Either way." She went back to her counting, then added, without looking up, "If you stay through opening weekend, I can shift you to mornings only in July. Then you'd have evenings for whatever else."

Amelia stood in the doorway doing arithmetic she had not expected to be doing. The camp wanted an answer by five o'clock. The whistle lanyard was still in her pocket from Thursday, coiled like something alive. She pulled it out, hung it back around her neck, and said, "Let me make one call before I decide anything."

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: A down payment is the part of a home's price the buyer pays upfront so less must be borrowed; in British usage it is called a deposit.
story:
The real estate office smelled of coffee and photocopier toner, and by four o'clock every Thursday it belonged mostly to Madison. She fed listings into the scanner, straightened the brochures in the rack by the window, and answered the phone when Ms. Virtanen was showing a house. In exchange she got twelve dollars an hour and a drawer in the back where she kept her savings envelope, forty-one weeks of pay folded into a rubber band. She had done the arithmetic on the bus so many times that the numbers had worn smooth: an apartment near campus, if she and Celia split it, meant first month's rent plus a damage deposit, and the deposit was the part you paid upfront and got back if you left the place undestroyed.

The trouble had arrived on Tuesday, when Celia spread three rental listings across Madison's bed and Coralie lay on the floor with her shoes off, doing the math on her phone. "It says here twelve hundred a month, plus deposit," Celia said. "So to move in we need twenty-four hundred. Minimum." Coralie said her cousin had gotten her deposit back minus eighty dollars for a carpet stain the size of a coin, which started a long argument about whether landlords monetized every scuff and scratch, turning ordinary wear into invoices. Madison had listened while feeling something loosen in her chest. Twenty-four hundred was more than her envelope held. She needed eleven more paydays, and the good apartments near campus would be gone by then.

So when a man came into the office on Thursday asking about the gray house on Fenwick Street, Madison paid attention. He was British, Ms. Virtanen said afterward, relocating for a job, and he leaned over the counter while Ms. Virtanen pulled up the listing. "Three forty-nine," she told him. "And you'd want to talk to a lender, but most buyers around here put down ten percent or so."

"Right, the deposit," the man said.

Madison, shelving brochures behind him, opened her mouth before she could think better of it. "The damage deposit?" she asked. "But it's not a rental."

The man turned around, and she felt her face go hot, but he only smiled. "We call it a deposit. The part you pay upfront so you borrow less." Ms. Virtanen nodded along, tapping the listing. "Here we'd usually say down payment," she said, "but same idea." Madison stood there with a brochure in each hand, rearranging something in her head. The word she had carried around for weeks, the word that meant money you scraped together and hoped to get back, meant something entirely different to the man at the counter: money you paid forward, on something that became yours.

After he left, she asked Ms. Virtanen whether she could sit in on a first meeting with a mortgage broker, and Ms. Virtanen, who believed teenagers learned by being allowed into rooms, said Friday at ten. So Madison missed study hall, and sat at the end of a conference table while a broker explained to a young couple that the bank would lend them most of the house's price but not all of it, that the gap was theirs to close, and that closing it made the monthly payments smaller for the next twenty-five years. The couple kept glancing at each other, doing silent arithmetic of their own, and Madison recognized the look. It was the look she and Celia had traded over the listings on the bed.

Walking back to school, she turned it over. A renter's deposit was a promise you'd behave; a down payment was a promise you'd stay, a wall of your own money standing between you and the bank's patience. Same word, opposite direction, and the direction was the whole point. She wondered which one she was actually saving toward, and whether wanting the second one at sixteen was ambition or just a bromide she'd absorbed from somewhere, one of those comfortable sayings about owning rather than throwing money away on rent. Rent wasn't thrown away, exactly. It bought a month of roof. But it bought nothing that stayed.

That evening Celia called. The apartment on Dunbar had fallen through, the landlord wanted a co-signer, and Celia's voice had the flat careful sound of someone deciding not to be upset yet. "So we keep looking," she said. "Or we don't. I don't know."

"I have an idea," Madison said. She pulled the rubber band off her envelope and counted the bills again on her desk, not because the number would have changed but because counting felt like a thing to do. Then she opened her laptop and typed the broker's name from the conference room, and beneath it, in the search bar, the words first time buyer. "It might take years," she said into the phone. "It might take years and we might change our minds. But can I at least show you what I found?" Celia said nothing for a moment, and then, quietly, "Yeah. Show me." Madison picked up the envelope and slid it into her backpack, next to her binder, where she could feel it through the canvas when she stood.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A note one octave higher than another vibrates at exactly twice its frequency, so the A above A440 is 880 hertz.
story:
Cohen had been carrying the double bass to Mr. Bekele's studio for three months now, and he still hadn't figured out how to get through the door. The instrument wanted to go in sideways; the doorframe disagreed. He shuffled, pivoted, and finally tipped the scroll through first, like a pelagic fish being landed through a hatch, which was exactly the kind of image Kim would have supplied if she'd been there to see it.

"Early again," said Mr. Bekele, not looking up from a ledger where he tracked who owed him what. "You are trying to preempt your own lesson. It will not work. Sit."

"I'm not early. I'm exactly on time."

"You are early. I can smell it on you." He put down his pencil. "Tuner, please."

That was the ritual. Cohen would pluck the open A string, and the little clip-on tuner would judge him with a needle. Today the needle sat flat, so Mr. Bekele had him turn the peg, a millimeter at a time, while the numbers on the tuner's face climbed. 436. 438. Then, with a pluck that felt no different from the last one, the screen settled: 440.

"There," said Mr. Bekele. "A. The world agrees with you now."

Cohen held the tuner in his palm and looked at the number for a long moment. He was thinking about last weekend, about Kim's living room and the electric keyboard she'd gotten from an uncle who bought things impulsively, like a man serving a subpoena against his own bank account. Kim had been noodling out a bassline and complaining that Cohen's open A sounded "sad" next to her synth, and he had told her, with the confidence of someone who had never checked, that her keyboard was wrong and the bass was right. He'd clipped his tuner to her music stand to prove it, and she'd played her A, and the screen had read 880, which he'd announced as evidence of total equipment failure. She'd laughed at him for ten straight seconds, which he felt he had earned.

Now he reached up the fingerboard, found the place where his teacher had shown him the A an octave higher, and plucked it. He watched the screen. 880. He plucked the open string again. 440. He did it twice more, as if the numbers might rearrange themselves out of embarrassment.

"Something is wrong?" Mr. Bekele asked.

"No. Something is right, I think, in a way I didn't know it could be." He held up the tuner. "Look. When I play the A up high, it reads exactly double. 880. The low one's 440." He plucked both again, slowly, like a man checking his own pockets. "It's the same note, but it's vibrating twice as fast. That's what makes it higher."

Mr. Bekele crossed the room and looked at the screen, hands folded behind his back like a customs officer. "Yes. And?"

"And Kim's keyboard wasn't broken. Her A was 880 because it was the higher one, and mine was 440 because mine's the low one, and I told her she needed to fix her synth. In front of Talia." He winced. "Talia filmed some of it."

"So this is not a lesson about octaves. This is a lesson about apology."

"It might be both," Cohen said. "They can be both."

Mr. Bekele made a sound that was nearly a laugh. "Then here is your assignment. Open A, then the octave, back and forth, ten times, listening. You will hear that they are the same letter and not the same sound. This is also true of people, but I am not allowed to say things like that, so I did not say it."

Cohen played the pair, 440 and 880, the low note round and dark under his fingers, the high one thinner, brighter, unmistakably kin. Somewhere in the middle of the eighth repetition he stopped worrying about whether he'd been wrong or only confident in the wrong direction, and started hearing the two As the way you hear two versions of one sentence, one told in a kitchen and one told at a funeral. Kim would want the whole story tonight, and Talia would want to play the video, and he would let her.

"Text her from the hallway," Mr. Bekele said, glancing at the clock. "And when you carry that fish out the door, remember it goes sideways."

Cohen tipped the scroll back through the frame, then stopped, still half in and half out of the room, and typed with his thumb: you were right, it vibrates exactly twice as fast, and I owe you a coffee. He pressed send before he could take it back.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: In mayonnaise, lecithin and proteins from egg yolk act as emulsifiers, holding tiny oil droplets suspended in water so the sauce does not separate.
story:
The Saturday market smelled like wet cilantro and burnt sugar from the kettle corn stand, and Layla moved through it with her grandmother's list folded into her back pocket. She had promised dinner tonight, the whole meal, because her mother had worked doubles all week and her father had been quiet in the way that Layla had learned to read as grief spread thin over months. Her grandfather had died in March. Tonight was the first time anyone had suggested the family eat his favorite meal since the funeral, and Layla had volunteered before she could think better of it.

She bought eggs from a woman with a hand-lettered sign reading PASTURED, and asked whether the yolks were dark. The woman lifted one from the carton to show her, orange as a persimmon. "Good ones for aioli," the woman said, and Layla nodded as if she had not been about to make mayonnaise from a video whose comments she had scrolled for forty minutes that morning, looking for reasons it might fail.

At the tomato stall she ran into Hasan, who was carrying a paper bag of padron peppers and eating one raw like an apple. He worked the market on weekends, hauling crates for the mushroom vendor, and he fell into step beside her easily, the way he did. When she told him about the dinner, he was quiet for a moment, then said, "You're going to eulogize him with salad dressing." It came out softer than it sounded written down, and she laughed before she could stop herself, and then felt the laugh sit strangely in her chest.

"It was his thing," she said. "He made it every Friday. He'd whisk it by hand and make everyone watch." That was true, though the fuller truth was that she had watched from the doorway more than once, and that the mayonnaise had been the one thing her grandfather had never let anyone help with, and that she had thought, this week, that making it might be like hearing him again. Hasan looked at her the way he looked at proofs he suspected were correct but unfinished. "Text me if it breaks," he said, and peeled off toward the mushroom stall.

Kallie found her at the honey table, where Layla was standing with her phone out, replaying the video for the third time. Kallie taught half the swim team and was the only person Layla knew who read instruction manuals cover to cover. She watched the video over Layla's shoulder and frowned. "You're starting with all the oil at once," she said. "That's the whole problem with people. They think a recipe is a suggestion." She believed in procedure, in steps followed in order, in the deep satisfaction of things done correctly. Layla believed, or had always believed, in improvisation, in tasting and adjusting, in the loose wrist her grandfather had and she did not. Between the two of them they bought the honey and a lemon and argued gently all the way to the parking lot about whether following rules was the same as understanding.

At home the kitchen was hot and still. Her mother had left a note that just said THANK YOU, with a heart, and Layla set out the bowl, the whisk, the jar of neutral oil, the beautiful orange yolks. She separated the eggs with her hands the way the video showed. She added the lemon and the salt and a teaspoon of water, and she began to drip oil, whisking, and for a while it worked: the mixture thickened, turned pale cream, clung to the wires of the whisk. It felt like a small sun in the bowl. She texted Kallie a photo with no caption and got back three exclamation points.

Then she got confident. She poured the oil in a thin stream, then a steadier one, and somewhere in the middle of wanting to be finished, wanting to shower before everyone came home, the sauce turned on her. It slackened, then went glossy and grainy, and when she stopped whisking, a pool of clear oil rose at the edges and the rest sat in a sullen lump at the bottom of the bowl, refusing to come together. She stood over it with her phone in one hand and did not text anyone. It seemed suddenly like something larger than a sauce, though she knew it was not, and knowing that did not help.

She started over with a fresh yolk, and this time she went too slow, so cautious that the emulsion never took at all, the oil simply floating free, and she had to pour the whole failure down the drain. The second bowl left a film on the porcelain like the sheen on the retention pond behind the school, where they had been told in assembly that the runoff sank toward the aquifer, the deep water under everything that the whole county drank from. Contained, or spoiled, depending. She rinsed the bowl and called her grandmother.

Her grandmother had been a chemist in Karachi before she was anything else in this country, and she did not comfort people over the phone, she asked questions. What exactly was in the bowl. How much oil, added how fast. Layla described it, the sudden loosening, the oil sitting on top, and her grandmother said, "You lost the suspension. The lecithin and the proteins in the yolk are what hold the tiny oil droplets suspended in the water so the sauce does not separate. Your droplets all joined together and the oil went its own way." Layla wrote it on the back of the receipt from the egg stall. "Can I fix it?" she asked. "It's broken, not ruined," her grandmother said. "Take a clean bowl. One fresh yolk. Whisk it with a little water until it's slack, then add your failed sauce to it, slowly, drop by drop. The new yolk will hold it." A pause, then, dry as always: "Your grandfather split his at least once a year, you know. He never told anyone but me."

So Layla did it. She dripped the failed sauce into a new yolk, whisking low and steady, and watched the broken thing become whole again, glossy and thick, exactly as thick as she remembered from those Fridays at the doorway. It was not the first egg's doing alone and not the second's; it was both, the rescue folded through the failure. She stood in the cooling kitchen holding the bowl and thinking about the difference between following a recipe and understanding one, and admitting to herself that she did not entirely know which she had done.

Her mother came in at six with her work shoes still on, and her father behind her, and they stood in the doorway the way Layla used to. She set the bowl on the table and dipped a spoon in and held it out. "It broke," she said, "and I fixed it." Her father took the spoon, and tasted, and closed his eyes.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: Without its natural greenhouse effect, Earth's average surface temperature would be about minus 18 degrees Celsius instead of roughly 14 degrees Celsius.
story:
The trail began behind the recycling depot and climbed through pines toward a lookout that the guidebook promised was "moderate," which was a word Christopher was beginning to distrust. In his backpack, along with a squashed sandwich and two water bottles, was the thing he was supposed to have mastered by Monday: a photocopied graph of carbon dioxide concentrations across the last century, its line stepping upward like a staircase into an attic, and a page of notes from Ms. Ahmed that read, in her tidy hand, "Explain the mechanism. Use the graph. No excuses this time."

"You could just read it tonight," Rex said, walking backwards in front of him with the confidence of someone who had never tripped over a root. "Instead you're carrying it up a mountain like a pilgrim."

"It's a hill," Christopher said. "And I read better when I'm moving. It's a documented phenomenon."

"It's a documented excuse," said Harley, who was hiking with the grim purpose of someone trying to reach the lookout before noon, because at noon she had promised to be at her brother's birthday party, and her mother, an autocrat of the birthday-cake variety, did not accept trailhead delays as a reason for anything.

At the first switchback Christopher stopped and unfolded the graph against a boulder. The paper fluttered. He pinned one corner with his water bottle and squinted at the small jagged rises and falls riding on top of the big smooth climb. "Okay, so this sawtooth part," he said. "That's the planet breathing, sort of. Every year. But the overall line just goes up."

"Obviously it goes up," Rex said. "Greenhouse gases are the villain. Villains make lines go up. That's how graphs work, I'm pretty sure."

"Except," Christopher said slowly, and then stopped, because the next part was the part he'd gotten wrong in class on Thursday, the part Ms. Ahmed had circled in red and written see me beside. He had said, confidently, in front of everyone, that greenhouse gases were basically a mistake of the modern world, a pollution thing, and that Earth would be better off without them entirely.

Harley looked over his shoulder, though not for long, because she was watching the sky for signs of noon. "What's the matter with that?"

"Ms. Ahmed asked me what the temperature would be with no greenhouse effect at all, and I said, I don't know, normal, maybe. She made this face." He recreated the face. It was a mild face, but a devastating one. "She wrote a number on the board and told me to think about the Moon."

"The Moon," Rex repeated, as though she had told him to think about cheese. He expostulated for a while about teachers and their riddles, about how if the answer was the Moon the question should just say the Moon, and while he went on, Christopher sat down on the boulder and did the actual thinking.

The Moon had no atmosphere worth mentioning. No blanket. Earth's average surface temperature, he'd since looked up, sat around fourteen degrees Celsius, which sounded unimpressive until you considered the alternative: without the natural greenhouse effect, the same surface would be about minus eighteen. Thirty-two degrees of warmth, furnished by gases that Rex wanted to cast as the villain of the story. The problem, he was starting to see, was not that the gases existed. The problem was the line on his graph, the line that kept climbing past anything natural, like a thermostat in the hands of someone who hadn't noticed they were still turning it.

"So they're not evil," he said out loud. "They're more like, insulation. A certain amount of insulation is why anything survives. It's the extra insulation we keep adding."

Rex stopped mid-sentence, which for Rex was a significant event. "That's a much worse story than mine," he complained. "You can't debate insulation. Villains are clean. Insulation is, what, a moral complexity? At a birthday party?"

"It's not about clean," Christopher said, though he privately conceded that his old version had been easier to hold in his head, one bad guy, one graph going up, case closed. The new version had a hinge in it. Gases you could not live without, and could not keep adding forever, and the difference between those two things was the whole argument, and it lived inside the same word.

Harley checked her phone. "Ten forty. You have two hours of my life, and then I become a bad sister." She pointed up the trail. "Walk and talk."

They walked. Christopher held the graph in one hand and used it like a map, which it sort of was, a map of where the air had been. "Look at this part," he said, tapping the sharp dip in the middle of one of the sawtooth years. "That's summer in the northern hemisphere, all the plants pulling carbon down. Then winter, and it climbs back. Every single year, down and up, down and up, like breathing. And the breathing never changes. But the baseline underneath it just rises. It's like the ground under the breathing is lifting."

"That's actually good," Harley said, grudgingly, because she was saving her approval for when it would sting Rex the most.

"What's still bothering you?" Rex asked, and Christopher appreciated that Rex, whatever his flaws, and his flaws were numerous and well-documented, could always tell when something was still bothering him.

"I don't know exactly where the line turns dangerous," Christopher admitted. "I know the shape of it. I know the planet needs some of this and we're adding more. But how much more, and how fast, and what that means for any particular place, any particular year, I'd be making it up if I said." He folded the graph along its worn crease. "Ms. Ahmed said a good explanation includes what you don't know. I thought she was being annoying. Now I think she meant it's the difference between an explanation and a slogan."

Rex considered this for approximately eight steps. "Fine. Monday I'll say it your way. But I'm keeping the villain thing as a metaphor, and you can't stop me."

They reached the lookout at eleven, which was early enough that Harley permitted herself four minutes of standing at the rail. Below them the valley sat under its enormous invisible blanket of air, fourteen degrees Celsius of borrowed warmth holding everything green and alive in place. Christopher looked at the pines, then at the folded paper in his pocket, then at the sky, which was doing its slow work over all of it without any opinion at all.

"Harley," he said. "For the party. Tell your brother the Moon is minus eighteen and we're not."

Harley shouldered her pack. "He's four," she said. "He'll be thrilled."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: The Islamic calendar is lunar and about 10 to 11 days shorter than the solar year, so Ramadan and Eid al-Fitr come roughly 10 to 11 days earlier each year.
story:
The morning of Eid, Aaron stood at the kitchen window watching grey light adumbrate the roofs across the street, the shapes coming forward slowly, half-formed, like an argument he hadn't finished. The house smelled of cardamom and frying onions. His mother moved through the kitchen in her good shalwar, and his father had already taken the good tray down from the top shelf, the one that only appeared for Eid and for funerals.

The problem sat in his pocket, folded twice: his exam schedule. Calculus, first thing tomorrow morning, and Eid today meant the whole day gone, the relatives, the food, the mosque, the visits that could not be shortened without insult. Last year Eid had fallen in the middle of July, when school was a distant memory and the fasting days stretched long into the evening. He had assumed, without ever thinking about it, that it would always be a summer thing, that Eid belonged to heat and hose-water and backyard tables.

"It moved," Lea-Maude had said on Thursday, squinting at his schedule over her shoulder in the library. She was not Muslim, but she kept track of things the way other people kept track of sports scores. "The Islamic calendar is lunar. It's about ten to eleven days shorter than the solar year, so Ramadan and Eid come roughly ten to eleven days earlier every year. That's why it's during exams this year when it was in summer before."

Aaron had stared at her. He had fasted every Ramadan since he was twelve and had somehow never assembled those facts into a picture. The month had simply appeared where it appeared, the way weather appeared. "Earlier every year," he'd repeated, and she'd nodded and gone back to her chemistry notes, and he had sat there feeling both stupider and more awake than usual.

Now, at the kitchen table, his younger cousins were already circling the dessert tray with an almost epicurean seriousness, sampling the baklava corner by corner to compare honey distribution. Coen had come over early, because Coen's family was two streets away and because Coen never needed a reason, only a door left unlocked. He dropped into the chair beside Aaron and stole a piece of semolina cake.

"So you're writing tomorrow," Coen said. It was not a question. Coen had a way of finding the soft spot in any plan.

"First thing. Nine a.m." Aaron turned his teacup a quarter turn, then another. "The month drifts back through the year, ten or eleven days at a time. Lea-Maude told me. It'll be in spring exams next time, and then before that." He was still turning the cup. The strange part was not the fact itself but the way it had been sitting under his own life, unnoticed, while he'd prayed and fasted and eaten his way through it.

"Do you want to leave early? Study tonight?"

Aaron looked down the table. His uncle was retelling the story of a Eid from twenty years ago in another country, a story that grew more elaborate with each year, and his mother was laughing with her whole face, the laugh she only had here. He could go upstairs with his calculus textbook and his nemesis, the integration unit that had been quietly defeating him since March. Or he could sit in this loud, sugary, obligated room and let the day be what it was intended to be, a breaking, a feast, an ending of a hard month.

"I'll study after dinner," he said. "The relatives leave at eight."

Coen raised an eyebrow. "The relatives never leave at eight."

"The relatives leave at eight," Aaron said again, and ate the cake.

He did get two hours in, near midnight, with the integration problems swimming in front of him while downstairs his father watched highlights with the volume low. He could not make the substitution work on the third problem, and he sat with that failure instead of fighting it, noticing how his mind kept drifting back to the drifting calendar, to the idea that something could be perfectly steady and still never arrive in the same place twice. Whether he would pass tomorrow, whether he had chosen the right portion of the day to give to each of his obligations, whether a festival that moved and a schedule that stood still could ever be made to agree: these things he did not know. He closed the book at one in the morning and set two alarms.

At breakfast his mother slid a plate toward him and said, "Eat properly. Eid leftovers are in your bag for after."

"For after the exam?"

"For after everything," she said, and wrapped the foil tighter around the edges.

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: Robert Millikan measured the charge of the electron by using the electric field between two horizontal charged plates to hold tiny charged oil drops still against gravity.
story:
The Millikan exhibit sat in the corner of the physics hall, between a plasma globe and a wall of oversized periodic tables, and Layla would have walked past it if Lorelai hadn't grabbed her sleeve. Under glass stood a replica of a brass chamber with two horizontal metal plates, one above the other, separated by maybe a hand's width, and beside it a small screen playing a loop of oil drops hanging in the space between them like beads suspended in nothing.

"Robert Millikan," Layla read off the placard, mostly to hear the name in her own mouth, "measured the charge of the electron by using the electric field between two horizontal charged plates to hold tiny charged oil drops still against gravity." She read it twice. The second time the sentence did something in her head, the way a word repeated too often stops sounding like a word and starts sounding like a mechanism.

"Is this on the quiz," Lorelai said, in the flat voice she used for genuine questions.

"Everything is on the quiz." Layla crouched to look through the side window of the replica. Somewhere in the exhibit's guts a pump hissed, and a fine mist of droplets drifted down through the gap, catching the light in little evanescent sparks before vanishing against the dark lower plate. She thought of her father's prayer beads, the way he moved them during Ramadan, thumb over thumb, the counting itself a kind of holding still.

The quiz was Thursday. Mr. Visser had written one problem on the board before the field trip and refused to solve it: two parallel plates, a potential difference, a separation distance, find the field strength at a point between them, then find the force on a charge placed there. Layla had copied it into her notebook and then, in the margin, copied it again in Arabic script, transliterating the variables letter by letter because sometimes her grandmother asked to see her schoolwork and Layla liked the look of the two alphabets side by side, the same problem wearing different clothes.

Macey found them by the exhibit, carrying a paper cone of popcorn she had smuggled out of the café in defiance of at least three signs. "You're doing homework at a museum," she said. "You're doing homework at a museum that has a tornado simulator."

"It's not homework, it's the same problem." Layla pulled out the notebook. "Look. Field strength, then force. The plates make a uniform field between them, so the same value works anywhere in the gap. If Millikan could hold a drop still, the electric force had to equal the weight. That's the whole trick. Nothing moves, so the two forces cancel." Even as she said it she heard how it sounded, like an explanation, and she stopped, embarrassed, as though she'd claimed something she hadn't earned yet.

Macey leaned over the glass, chewing. "So how do you actually get the number?"

"You divide the potential difference by the distance between the plates." Layla heard herself say it and checked it against the placard, against the loop on the screen, against the drop hanging there. It hung. That was the proof, a drop the size of a dust mote doing arithmetic she'd only just learned to do herself. "Then force is field times charge. So if you know the force, because the drop isn't falling, you can get the charge. That's how he measured it."

Mr. Visser appeared at her shoulder with the timing of a man who had been pretending not to listen. He smelled of the coffee he wasn't supposed to have in the hall. "And what would happen," he said, "if the field were too strong?"

Layla looked at the drop. She understood the question was a door and that he was holding it open, and she resented him a little for it, the artifice of the Socratic method, the teacher's oldest trick dressed up as curiosity. "The drop would go up," she said. "Too weak, it falls. Right value, it floats."

"Thursday," he said, and drifted toward the plasma globe, where a group of ninth graders was trying to make the lightning follow someone's finger.

They spent another hour in the hall. Macey lost a quarter to the tornado simulator's coin spiral and declared the whole building a scam. Lorelai photographed the periodic table wall for reasons she declined to state. Layla sat on the bench across from the Millikan replica with her notebook open, working the problem in both scripts, and the numbers came out the same both times, which they were always going to, but which still felt like a small mercy, proof that something could be true in more than one language.

She wrote the final answer and underlined it, then sat looking at the hanging drop, at the balance she had computed on paper happening in brass and oil ten feet away. She had the number. What she didn't have was any sense of why the universe bothered to keep its books so exactly, why a field should be so obediently uniform, why charge came in units at all, and she suspected Mr. Visser didn't either, and suspected further that this was the thing none of them would say out loud on Thursday.

The lights in the hall dimmed for the four o'clock cycle. The loop on the screen reset, the drops began again their slow descent, caught, held, released.

"Same answer in Arabic?" Lorelai asked, looking over her shoulder.

"Same answer," Layla said, and closed the notebook as the first drop caught the light.

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
knowledge_domain: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
fact: In SQL, comparing anything to NULL with '=' never returns true, even NULL = NULL; you must test with IS NULL instead.
story:
The public library on Delancey had a computer lab in the basement that smelled of carpet glue and old radiator, and Olivia had claimed the corner terminal for two hours every Saturday since September. She was there because Mr. Torres had announced, with the flat enthusiasm of a man reading from a memo, that the students who finished his data elective would build something a local business could actually use. The bakery on Seventh wanted to know which customers had stopped coming in. Olivia had volunteered, mostly to have something to put on applications that sounded less like everyone else's, and partly because the bakery gave volunteers a free pastry on Thursdays, a detail Mr. Torres had mentioned in the same tone he used for everything else.

The problem turned out to be harder than the pastry had implied. She had two tables, customers and orders, and she needed the customers who appeared in the first and not the second.
