She'd found something called a LEFT JOIN online, which seemed to promise exactly this, and she'd written a WHERE clause to filter the result. Karan sat beside her with his chair tipped back at an angle the librarians had given up policing, eating sunflower seeds out of his jacket pocket with a concentration he did not extend to his schoolwork.

"Show me the query," he said, spitting a shell into his palm.

She turned the screen. "The join works. It gives me everybody, with blanks for the people who never ordered. Then I filter for the blanks. WHERE order_id equals NULL. But it returns zero rows, and I know there are at least four people who haven't ordered anything, because I asked."

Karan leaned in, and for a moment his chair found all four of its legs. He was quiet in a way that Olivia had learned to distrust, since his silences usually preceded either a correct answer or a claim that he'd once met a rapper's cousin. "Zero rows," he said. "Not the four."

"Zero. Like the table's empty, except I can see it isn't."

He scrolled her result set, all the joined rows with their blank order columns, and she watched his finger stop on one. The blank sat there in its cell, unbothered. There was something almost smug about it, she thought, the way it refused to be caught.

"Try IS," he said finally.

"Is what?"

"Not equals. IS. WHERE order_id IS NULL."

She typed it, and the table repopulated itself with four names, one of which was Mrs. Okafor from the end of her street, who had apparently signed up for the bakery's loyalty program and then never bought a single thing, a fact that struck Olivia as its own small biography. She sat back. "Why does that work?"

"Because comparing anything to NULL with equals never returns true," Karan said. "Even NULL equals NULL doesn't. You have to use IS NULL." He put another seed in his mouth. "I read it at two in night, don't ask why."

"So my query was asking a question that had no answer."

"That's a dramatic way to put it."

"I'm a dramatic person."

This was not entirely true. Olivia's drama was mostly internal, and it was currently staging a small argument about the four names on her screen. The bakery wanted to lure these people back, Mr. Torres had said, with coupons or a postcard or whatever the students designed. But the data didn't say why they'd never ordered. Mrs. Okafor might be gluten intolerant and loyal to the bakery anyway, in which case a coupon was a taunt. She might have signed up at a moment of optimism and never returned to it, which was a condition Olivia recognized from her own relationship with several notebooks. The query found the absence, and the absence was real, but its meaning sat underneath, in a layer the database didn't have.

She said some version of this out loud, minus the notebooks. Karan considered it while cracking a seed between his teeth. "So what do you want to do?"

"I want to give them a list of four people and not pretend the list explains anything." She pulled the keyboard toward her again. "I'll write it up. Who they are, what they ordered, which is nothing, and what we don't know."

"That's going to be a short presentation."

"It'll be an honest one."

The word substrate had come up in her chemistry class that week, some layer underneath a reaction where the real work happened, and she thought about it now as she saved her query. The names were the surface. The reasons were the substrate, present but unqueried, and no join she could write would reach them. She suspected Mr. Torres would say this was fine, would say the data does what it does, and she suspected she would half believe him and half not, and that the half that didn't would be the more useful half to carry into whatever she ended up doing after June.

When the lab's lights flickered their ten-minute warning, Karan stood and stretched with the satisfaction of a man who had contributed. "Tell them the NULL thing," he said. "It'll beguile them. People love a rule that breaks their brains."

"People love that?"

"I love that."

She copied her results onto a flash drive, labeled the file in the way she'd learned to, with the date and a plain name, and dropped it into her bag next to the paperback she was never quite reading. At the top of the stairs, the library's main floor was closing down, the shelves going dark in sections, and through the front window the bakery's sign was visible two blocks off, its neon steady, its door shut for the night. Mrs. Okafor's house, Olivia happened to know, was on her way home.

She stood a moment with her hand on the door bar. Then she pushed it, and turned left instead of right.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: German capitalizes every noun, not only names, which helps a reader of a German article spot the nouns in a sentence at a glance.
story:
The newspaper had cost Sarah two euros and fifty cents at the kiosk by the U-Bahn station, and she had bought it because her host father had announced, cheerfully and in front of everyone, that she would summarize one article aloud at Sunday breakfast. Sunday breakfast was eighteen hours away. She spread the paper across the desk in her small rented room, where the radiator ticked and smelled faintly of dust and warm metal, and counted the capitalized words in the first paragraph. She counted twenty-three. In English that would have been a paragraph shouting at her, all names and titles and beginnings of sentences, but this was German, and something was going on that nobody had warned her about.

She texted Larissa, who was back home in her ordinary bedroom with her ordinary summer job. "Did you know German capitalizes basically everything?" The reply came fast: "Everything?" Sarah scrolled back through the article. Not everything. Verbs stayed lowercase. So did most of the little connector words, the ands and ins and ofs. It was the nouns. She tested it against a sentence she could half parse, one about a strike at the airport: the word for airport was capitalized, the word for delayed was not, the word for passengers was. Every noun wore a capital, not just the names of people and places. It was as if the language had tagged its nouns with small flags so a beginner could find them. She sat with that for a moment, feeling the article rearrange itself on the page, the nouns rising up out of the morass of unfamiliar endings and letting the rest of the sentence sink beneath them.

Downstairs, Mr. Gill, the retired teacher who owned the house and rented rooms to students and summer guests, was rinsing teacups in the kitchen. He was English, had lived in Munich for thirty years, and spoke German like water. Sarah brought the newspaper down and pointed at a headline about a politician whose speech had been described as scathing. "Herr Gill," she said, and then, correcting herself because he had asked her to, "Mr. Gill. Why does this word have a capital? It's not a name." He dried his hands slowly, the way he did everything, and said, "German capitalizes every noun, not only names." Then he picked up his tea and went to his chair by the window, because he believed, as he had told her the first night, that students learn nothing from answers that arrive too complete. What she did with his one sentence was her own business.

What she did with it was go back upstairs and try to read. The article she chose was short, five paragraphs, about a plan to charge a fee for plastic bags, and it contained a quote from a shopkeeper who worried that smaller stores would be stigmatized as the dirty ones while the big chains bought their way to a green image. Sarah could not have defined every word, but the capitalized nouns came at her in a chain, almost like a list of the story's bones: fee, bags, chains, stores, customers, environment. She wrote them in her notebook in a column, then added the few verbs she recognized underneath, and found she could sketch the argument the way you sketch a face from its skeleton. It was not translation. It was something more like eavesdropping through a wall, catching the shape of a quarrel without every word.

The cost arrived at midnight, or near it. Her summary was due at nine in the morning, spoken aloud, and when she tried to say the sentence she had built, her mouth tripped over the noun flags she had been so grateful for on the page. She could see them; she could not say them. The word for environment sat in her throat like a stone. She texted Brennen, who was on the same exchange program two streets over and had been assigned the same breakfast torture. "Can you pronounce Umwelt?" His voice note came back garbled by the hotel wifi, but at the end he laughed, a real laugh, and said, "I have been saying it as oom-welt for an hour and my host sister says I am describing a type of sausage." Sarah laughed too, alone in the ticking room, and then said the word to the radiator until the radiator seemed to accept it.

By two in the morning she had a spoken summary of about ninety seconds: the fee, the chains, the shopkeeper's fear of being stigmatized, the environment. It was honest and it was small. She knew what she was leaving out, which was most of the article's nuance, the counterarguments, the numbers she could not confirm because her German stopped at the edge of anything figurative. She fell asleep with the light on and the newspaper on the floor, its nouns still standing at attention.

Breakfast was bread, cheese, jam, and coffee so strong it made her eyes water on the first sip. The host family arranged themselves around the table, and the host father, who had the cheerful cruelty of a man who assigns tasks and then enjoys them, said, "Sarah. Our newspaper." The room smelled of coffee and rye. Sarah put her hands flat on the table so they would not shake, and began. The first sentence came out crooked, the second nearly collapsed, and then she found the rhythm of it, halting but hers: the fee, the bags, the chains, the shopkeeper who did not want his shop looked down on, the environment, which everyone said they wanted to protect and no one wanted to pay for.

The host mother asked a follow-up question, something quick and long, and Sarah understood perhaps half of it, enough to know it was a real question and not a kindness. She said, "Können Sie das wiederholen?" and the host mother repeated it more slowly, and Sarah answered two sentences of the three it probably deserved. The eldest son, seventeen and merciless in the way of boys who have never had to be a beginner in anything, grinned at his plate. Mr. Gill, who had come down for coffee in his own house across the hall, said nothing at all, but he poured her a second cup before she had asked.

Afterward she carried the newspaper out to the front step, where the morning was already warm and a delivery cyclist rang his bell twice at the corner. She read the headline again, the one about the scathing speech, and this time she caught a noun she had missed, buried mid-sentence, and she said it aloud, quietly, to the street. Down the sidewalk the cyclist rang his bell again, and Sarah stood up with the paper under her arm and went to look for tomorrow's kiosk.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: The word blocking comes from 19th-century directors such as W. S. Gilbert, who planned scenes on a model stage using a block for each actor.
story:
Claire spread the coins across her grandmother's dining room table because the living room carpet had swallowed the last of her patience. Two afternoons of rehearsal had collapsed into the same argument: Jaiveer planted himself centre stage like a lamppost, and Zoya kept drifting toward the window, and neither of them believed her when she said the scene needed shape before it needed feeling.

"You're directing with adjectives," Zoya had told her, half laughing, half not, and the sentence had followed Claire home and then followed her here, to her grandmother's house, where the drama camp showcase was tolerated because her grandmother liked the noise.

The table was mahogany, large enough for ten diners, and Claire set a quarter where the doorway of the set would be and a nickel for the armchair and then, hesitantly, two loonies for the actors. She moved them. Jaiveer's loonie crossed to the window at the line about the letter; Zoya's loonie turned a quarter-circle to face him. It was small and slightly ridiculous, and it mesmerized her anyway, the whole scene legible in miniature, like reading sheet music for bodies.

Her grandmother came through with tea and stopped, spectacles low on her nose. "What's this, then, treasure?"

"Rehearsal," Claire said. "Small scale." She slid Jaiveer's coin two inches left. "I couldn't get them to move, so now I move them instead."

Her grandmother made an approving noise and settled into the chair to watch, the way she watched everything, without hurry. On the sideboard behind her lay the old Britannica volume, the one Claire had pulled down the night before looking for anything on staging. Halfway through the theatre entry she had found it, a paragraph she'd read three times: nineteenth-century directors, W. S. Gilbert among them, planned their scenes on a model stage, placing a block for each actor. That was where the word came from, the book said. Blocking. Claire had sat very still on the hallway floor with the weight of the encyclopedia open across her knees, feeling both clever and late, as if she'd reinvented a wheel that had been rolling for a hundred and fifty years.

When the others arrived the next afternoon, she had the table ready. Zoya came in first, carrying her script rolled like a baton, and went straight to the coins. "What are these?"

"That's you," Claire said, tapping the smaller loonie. "That's Jaiveer. Watch." She walked the scene with her fingers, coin by coin, and Zoya leaned in, unrolled her script, and for a moment stopped performing being interested and simply was interested.

Jaiveer arrived morose, shoes wet from the short walk from the bus stop, mumbling about the rain and about Mr. Fitzgerald, the retired teacher next door, who had told him over the fence that the ending of the one-act was sentimental. "He said the mother forgiving her is cheap," Jaiveer said, dropping onto the couch. "He said real forgiveness takes longer than ten minutes."

"He read it over your shoulder while he was watering tomatoes," Zoya said. "That's not a review, that's eavesdropping."

"Maybe it's still right."

Claire let them have it, because she'd been circling the same doubt herself. She moved the coins through the final scene once, twice, and the problem surfaced without her naming it: the reconciliation happened face to face and too still, two people standing in the same spot exchanging feelings, exactly what the audience could get from a telephone call. "Try it there," she said, setting Zoya's coin behind the armchair, facing away. "She says it while she's leaving. She doesn't get to see what it does to you."

Zoya went quiet. She had wanted the reconciling scene from the beginning, had angled for it, Claire realized slowly, since the first read-through; she had underlined her speeches in pencil so many times the paper had gone grey. And now Claire was taking the face-to-face away from her, giving her a doorway and a turned back.

"Nobody will see my face," Zoya said.

"Everyone will hear you," Claire said. "And they'll watch his."

Zoya looked at the nickel that stood for the armchair, at the loonie she'd been given, and Claire understood that she was weighing something larger than blocking, something about whether a voice alone was enough. Then Zoya picked up her coin and set it exactly where Claire had placed it, pressing it down once, as if sealing it. "From the hallway, then," she said. "And I stop at the door for the last line. One beat. Then I go."

They ran it with their bodies instead of their money. Jaiveer sat in the armchair and did not move when the forgiveness came, and his stillness was worth more than anything he'd done in two afternoons of planting himself; the audience, Claire saw, would be watching him not knowing what to do with his hands. Zoya stopped in the doorway, one beat, and the rain ticked against the windows of her grandmother's house, and the room smelled of tea and the lemon polish the old woman put on the mahogany every Friday.

Afterward Jaiveer stood at the table looking at the little bronze population of the scene. "Mr. Fitzgerald says Gilbert did this," he said. "Used blocks on a model stage. That's why they call it blocking."

"I know," Claire said, and Zoya laughed at her, delighted, and Claire laughed too, because the wheel was old and she was new and the scene had finally moved.

Her grandmother came in with a plate of shortbread and paused at the table, counting the coins with her finger. "The ending's better," she said. "Though I don't know as I'd forgive so fast." She set down the plate and looked at Claire over her spectacles. "Move her one more time."

Claire slid Zoya's loonie half an inch toward the door.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: At Lunar New Year, many Chinese families give money in red envelopes to children and unmarried younger relatives, because red is associated with good fortune and warding off evil.
story:
The line for the dumplings went twice around the folding tables, and Connor's mother had already claimed four chairs near the stage, draping her coat over them like flags on territory. He had been told to help at the front desk of the cultural center until the lion dance started, collating the printed programs so that each stack held the schedule, the raffle ticket, and the sheet of paper lanterns for the children to fold. It was the kind of task that emptied his mind, and he was grateful for it, because otherwise he would have been watching the door.

The red envelopes had arrived that morning in a shoebox, brought by his great-aunt, who was now stationed at the corner table with a thermos of tea. All afternoon he had watched her press them into the hands of younger cousins, the small cousins, the ones who still shrieked when the drums started. He knew what the envelopes meant. He had known since he was six. What he did not know was whether seventeen counted.

Sukhman appeared at the desk around four, still wearing his debate team lanyard, and leaned on it. "Mr. Çelik sent me," he said. "He said you'd need hands for the programs."

"He said that because he doesn't want to do it himself." Connor slid a stack across. Mr. Çelig was the neighbor who volunteered at the center every weekend and was an expert at delegating whatever he found tedious.

They worked in a rhythm, Sukhman sorting, Connor stacking, and the stacks grew into tidy brick shapes. Sukhman watched the great-aunt for a while, then said, "So she just gives money to everyone under some age?"

"Roy said it's only for little kids," Connor said. "He got very confident about it. You know how he gets."

"Doctrinaire Roy," Sukhman agreed. "He has a position on everything before he has the facts." He flipped a raffle ticket into the wrong pile, unbothered. "But I don't actually know the rule either. This is like the ontology question from philosophy club. Like, who exists in the category. Who is a child."

"That's not what ontology means."

"It's close enough for a Friday." Sukhman squared his pile against the table edge. "You could just ask her."

Connor said he would rather not, which was not quite the truth. The truer version was that if he asked and the answer was no, the thing would be over, decided, filed away with the rest of childhood, whereas if he did not ask, he could carry the not-knowing like a coin in his pocket, and it still might turn up either way.

Then his cousin Mei, who was eight, ran past the desk holding her envelope aloft, and behind her came the great-aunt, moving slowly, one hand on the table for balance. She stopped in front of Connor. She looked at him for a long moment, the way she looked at everyone, as though verifying something against an old record.

"You are still in school," she said. It was not a question. She held out the envelope, red and crisp, with his name on it in her careful penmanship. "Red is good fortune. It wards off evil. You take it while you are young."

"I'm seventeen," Connor said, and heard how it sounded, like a disclaimer.

She did not lower her hand. "Not married," she said. "Still young. Take it."

Behind him Sukhman made a small noise that was almost certainly a laugh being strangled, and Connor took the envelope. It was lighter than he expected and warmer in his palm than the paper had any reason to be. The great-aunt patted his wrist once and moved on toward the stage, where the drums had begun their slow preliminary thunder.

"Roy is going to be insufferable when he's wrong," Sukhman said.

"He'll say he was right in spirit." Connor slid the envelope into his jacket, then took it out again and held it, because putting it away felt like dismissing it. He had spent the whole afternoon rehearsing a gracious refusal, a small speech about being too old, and now the speech was useless and he felt relieved and slightly foolish at once, the way you do when a door you'd braced your shoulder against simply swings open.

The lion appeared at the back of the hall, silk and sequins, blinking under the fluorescent lights, and the children screamed with delight and the great-aunt settled into one of the chairs his mother had guarded. Mei came back through the crowd and seized Connor's sleeve, pulling him toward the front, and he let himself be pulled, the envelope still in his hand.

activity: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
knowledge_domain: how rent, mortgages, deposits and down payments work when someone pays for a place to live
fact: A mortgaged home is collateral for the loan, so if the borrower stops paying, the lender can foreclose, taking and selling the home to recover the debt.
story:
Payton had been late to her first day at the office because she'd stopped at the mailbox on Ashland and read the notice taped to the door of the blue house. FORECLOSURE, it said, in letters she'd only ever seen on the news. She'd stood there long enough to be late, thinking about the man who lived there, the one who'd given her and her sister full chocolate bars every Halloween instead of fun-size.

At the real estate office, Ms. Bouchard handed her a stack of listing sheets and a pen that ran dry halfway through the first page. "You'll get used to the pens," Ms. Bouchard said. "Nobody replaces them. It's the one idiosyncrasy of this place I've stopped fighting."

There were three desks and only two agents. Payton sorted listings by price, then by neighborhood, then, when she got bored, by how much she'd want to live in each one. Johnny arrived at noon with applications for the apartment complex on Delmore, where he'd been trying to rent a two-bedroom with two friends since June.

"Tell me again why this is hard," Payton said, squinting at his paperwork.

"Because they want first month, last month, and a security deposit," Johnny said. "So to move into a place that costs eleven hundred a month, I need thirty-three hundred up front. I have nineteen." He tapped the deposit line. "And that's before the credit check, which I will fail, because I have no credit. You can't build credit without someone giving you credit first. It's a loop."

Payton looked down the application at the field marked monthly rent and then at the section in small print about what happened if he paid late. It seemed strange to her that a person could be charged money for not having money, but she said nothing, because she hadn't been invited to have opinions yet. She was there to file.

Gianna came in at three for her own reason, which she announced from the doorway: "My parents want to buy instead of rent, and they want me to understand it, so they sent me to bother a professional."

Ms. Bouchard, on the phone, pointed at the conference table without breaking her sentence.

They sat. Gianna spread out a folder of printed listings with prices circled in gel pen. "Here's what I don't get," she said. "The house is three hundred thousand dollars. We don't have three hundred thousand dollars. Nobody has three hundred thousand dollars. So how does anyone buy a house?"

"The bank has it," Payton said, mostly to test the thought. "The bank gives you the money, and then you pay the bank back every month, with interest. That's a mortgage. My parents have one. It's like renting money instead of renting an apartment, except it goes on for thirty years."

"Then what does the bank get if you don't pay it back?"

Payton opened her mouth and then closed it, because she had started to say I don't know, and then the word FORECLOSURE had surfaced in her mind, white letters on a blue door. "The house," she said slowly. "The house is the collateral. That's why the bank is willing to lend that much. If you stop paying, the lender can foreclose. They take the house and sell it to get their money back."

Gianna looked at her circled prices differently now. "So the people who lose their jobs..."

"Can lose the house too," Payton said. She was thinking of the blue house on Ashland, and how she'd walked past it every day for years and never once thought about whose money it was standing on.

When Ms. Bouchard hung up, she came over and slid a calculator across the table. She told Gianna about down payments, how her parents would need a percentage saved up front to prove to the lender they could commit, and how the bigger the down payment, the smaller the mortgage, the smaller the monthly payment. Gianna wrote numbers until the gel pen ran dry, and Payton thought of Johnny's nineteen hundred dollars and the loop he couldn't get out of. The two systems sat side by side in her head. Renting demanded everything at once and returned nothing. Buying demanded even more at once but, if nothing went wrong, returned something that accumulated. If something went wrong, it could take the roof with it.

She'd spent the summer arguing with her mother about moving into the dorms versus staying home and saving. Her mother's side was arithmetic. Payton's side had been about something she couldn't name, and she'd assumed that made it weaker. Now, watching Gianna add up thirty years of payments, she wasn't sure the arithmetic settled anything by itself. It was possible both things were true at once, that her mother was right about the money and wrong about the rest, and that Payton would only find out which mattered more by choosing and being wrong in one direction or the other. That part stayed open, and she let it stay open.

"Johnny," she called across the office. "Your dad's brother, the one with the house in the family. Would he co-sign?"

Johnny looked up. "He co-signed my cousin's car loan. Why."

"Because if the deposit and the credit are the loop, then the loop needs a second entrance." She turned his application around on the desk and set it beside Gianna's folder, the rental and the mortgage side by side, the two ways of paying for shelter in the same small office under the same bad fluorescent light.

Johnny picked up his phone. "Calling him now."

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: Stage directions in a script are usually set apart in italics or parentheses so actors and directors can tell them from spoken lines.
story:
Keira wrote the first draft of her play in the cafeteria of a university she had never seen before, between rounds of the debate tournament, on the back of a flow pad. Mr. Côté had assigned it in September: a ten-minute play, one moment from her own life, due to the community theatre's young writers' night in November, and he had refused to extend the deadline even when she pointed out that the tournament fell on the same weekend as the drafting. "Write it between rounds," he said. "Debaters are always claiming they can argue anything under pressure." She had told him that was fine, that she wasn't worried, and she kept telling herself that all the way through the bus ride, though she had written nothing in three weeks.

The moment she chose was small. Two Octobers ago, her mother had driven her to a hospital pharmacy at eleven at night and neither of them had said anything for the whole drive, and at the red light her mother had reached over and fixed Keira's collar, twice, though it wasn't crooked. She did not want to write about the diagnosis, or even name it. She wanted the play to be only the drive and the collar and the silence, and she suspected, in a way she could not yet predicate clearly, that the audience would understand the larger thing better if she never stated it. In debate she had been trained to state everything, to signpost, to say "therefore" until the word went thin. This was the opposite discipline and she did not yet know its rules.

Her first round was against a girl from a private school whose case was immaculate and whose delivery was laconic, almost bored, which unnerved Keira more than shouting would have. Keira won the round on speaker points and lost, she suspected, on substance, and she took the ballot to the cafeteria to read it alone. Sameer found her there anyway, sliding his own flows across the table, and Alix sat down a minute later with two cartons of chocolate milk and no explanation for the second one, setting it in front of Keira like it had always been hers.

"Read me something," Alix said. Keira covered the page with her arm. "It's bad." "Then it matches your record." Sameer snorted. Keira read them the opening anyway, flat, without performance, and when she reached the mother's first line she read straight through a sentence that was not dialogue at all, a sentence describing the mother turning up the heater, and Alix frowned. "Wait, does she say that out loud?" "No, it's just, it happens." "Then how would an actor know it's not a line?"

Keira looked at the page. She had written everything in the same hand, same margin, same unbroken lines, dialogue and description flowing together like a transcript of the whole car. She wrote, in pencil, the words "stage directions?" beside the heater sentence, and underlined nothing, and resolved to look it up, and then round two was called and she put the play away and went and argued about carbon taxes for forty minutes.

That night, in the hotel room she shared with Alix, she looked it up on her phone while Alix showered. Stage directions in a script are usually set apart in italics or parentheses so actors and directors can tell them from spoken lines. She read it twice, then opened her drafts app and typed it into the notes field, verbatim, the way she saved debate evidence. Then she texted her mother, because the theatre had emailed that the first read-through was Sunday afternoon, directly after the tournament's final round, and her mother would have to drive her straight there.

"Sunday works," her mother wrote back. "Is the play about us?" Keira typed "no" and deleted it, typed "partly" and deleted that too. "It's about a car ride," she sent finally, and her mother replied with a single thumbs-up, and Keira stared at that small yellow hand for a long time, unable to decide whether it meant her mother had understood everything or nothing. Alix came out of the bathroom with her hair dripping and asked who she was texting, and Keira said nobody, and locked the phone, and Alix looked at her for a second longer than the lie deserved and said only, "Your towel's on the floor."

Sunday, the community theatre's back room smelled of dust and hot glue. Four actors sat around a folding table with the copies Keira had printed that morning at the hotel business center, and she had done what the note had told her, mostly, except that in her hurry she had put parentheses around some directions and left others plain, trusting the italics of her laptop to survive printing, which it had not. A man in his fifties, playing the mother, read the second page fluently until he hit a plain-printed direction and delivered it, warmly and sincerely, as dialogue: "She reaches over and fixes her daughter's collar, twice."

The room went quiet. A younger actor started to laugh and caught it. Keira's face burned, and she heard herself say, quickly, "That's not a line, I'm sorry, it's a stage direction, they're supposed to be set off, italics or parentheses, and my italics didn't print," and the man waved his hand, unbothered, and marked his copy with a pen, and said, "Happens at half the read-throughs I do." She looked down at her pages and saw the whole script differently: two lineages of text, one meant for the voice and one meant for the body, and she had been treating them as one thing all along.

They read it again from the top. When they reached the collar moment, the man did not speak; he leaned over the empty chair beside him and mimed the small gesture, twice, and the actress playing Keira's part sat very still and let it happen to her, and something in the room tightened that no spoken line could have produced. Afterward the director asked what the silence was about, what the mother was fixing, what Keira had actually intended, and Keira opened her mouth to explain the diagnosis, the pharmacy, the whole buried architecture of the drive. Then she closed it. "I don't know yet," she said, and meant it, and the director nodded and wrote something in the margin of the script.

activity: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
knowledge_domain: to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question
fact: A preprint is a paper posted publicly before peer review, so its findings have not yet been checked by independent experts chosen by a journal.
story:
The writing club met on Tuesdays in the library's back room, where the radiator clanked like something trying to get out. Christopher spread his two articles across the table: one from a journal called Coastal Governance Quarterly, and one printed from a website he'd found at midnight, orange header, watermark faint across every page. His assignment, given by Mr. Desir last week, was to write a critical review comparing two scholarly articles on the same question. The question was whether beach nourishment, pumping sand onto eroding shores, actually protected coastal towns or just delayed the bill.

"You look like you're losing a war," Brooklyn said, dropping into the chair across from him. She unwrapped a sandwich she had clearly been saving through last period.

"I might be." He slid the orange-header paper toward her. "Look at the bottom of the first page."

Brooklyn read, chewing. "It says 'preprint.'" She said the word slowly, like tasting it. "What's that?"

Christopher had asked himself the same thing at one in the morning, and the answer he'd found had sat in his notes all day. "A preprint is a paper posted publicly before peer review," he said. "So its findings haven't been checked yet by independent experts chosen by a journal." He heard how rehearsed it sounded and didn't care. The fact had a shape to it, like a stone in his pocket.

The journal article, meanwhile, had passed through reviewers, an editor, revisions, a whole apparatus he'd never pictured before. It argued, with tidy regressions, that nourishment projects paid off for municipalities that could impute long-term tourist revenue to a wider beach, that the numbers justified the cost. The preprint argued the opposite: that the benefits were capricious, that a single storm season could erase the sand, and that the polity footing the bill, taxpayers, basically, was being sold a comfortable fiction. Same question, same data in some cases, opposite conclusions. Which one was he supposed to trust?

He flashed back to September, the first club meeting, when Mr. Desir had read aloud a review so cautious it said nothing at all, and then told them, "A good reviewer takes a position. Hedging is just fear wearing a blazer." Christopher had written that down. Now it seemed like a dare.

Brooklyn, meanwhile, was not there for philosophy. She had a submission deadline Friday for a citywide essay contest, the prize being five hundred dollars and a byline in the actual newspaper, and she wanted him to read her draft tonight. That was her whole reason for sitting here, sandwich and all. So he read it, and it was good, sharp and funny, about the school's dress code, except she had quoted a statistic from a source that turned out to be, when he checked his phone, somebody's blog.

"Where'd you get this number?" he asked.

"A teacher mentioned it once." She frowned at his screen. "So it's not real?"

"It might be real. It's just not checked by anyone." And that was when the two problems folded into each other, the way ideas sometimes did, like paper creasing along an old line. Brooklyn's blog number and his orange preprint were not the same thing, exactly, but they rhymed. Both were claims out in the world without a gate. The difference, he realized, was that the preprint was written by people trying to be checked, wanting the gate, just not there yet.

So that became his position, the one he started drafting right there while Brooklyn cut the statistic and rewrote her paragraph around what she could actually verify: the preprint wasn't worthless, and it wasn't equal to the journal article either. He would weight it differently, say so plainly, and admit what stayed uncertain, whether its argument would survive review or get shredded by it. Mr. Desir drifted over near the end, read two paragraphs standing up, and tapped the page. "This sentence," he said. "This one's honest."

Brooklyn packed up first, sliding her draft across the table. "Read the ending one more time before I send it. You're better at last lines."

Christopher looked at his own screen, then at hers, and pulled her pages toward the lamp. "Okay," he said. "From the top."

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: The Suzuki method, developed by Japanese violinist Shinichi Suzuki, teaches children to play by ear before reading music, the way they learn to speak before reading.
story:
Naomi had been reading music since she was eight, and by now the notation felt almost like handwriting, so quick that she sometimes forgot the notes were symbols at all. That was why she stalled in the doorway of the music classroom after school, her violin case bumping her hip. A small boy, maybe nine, stood at the front beside Mr. Popescu's desk playing the melody from the grade six book, the one Naomi had spent three weeks on, and playing it cleanly, his small fingers finding the shifts without hesitation. On the music stand in front of him, the page was upside down.

"He can't read a note," said Saif, who was sprawled in the back row waiting for the ensemble rehearsal to start. "I asked him. He stared at the page like it was a wall."

Naomi sat down two chairs away from the boy and watched. When he finished, he lowered the violin and looked at the floor, and she realized he was waiting for the next piece to be played to him, not handed to him. She wondered what that would feel like, to hold a whole melody in your ear the way you hold a sentence someone said to you, before any of it touched paper. She thought of her own first years: her mother taping flashcards of quarter notes to the kitchen cabinets, the endless decoding. Two roads into the same music, she thought, and neither of them seemed obviously better.

"How'd you learn that one?" she asked the boy. He shrugged and said his teacher hummed it and he copied it, then hummed it again. "It's the Suzuki method," Saif offered from behind them. "My little sister does it. Shinichi Suzuki, the Japanese violinist who came up with it."

"But you can't read anything?" Naomi said, and immediately worried it sounded like an accusation. The boy shook his head, unbothered, already plucking at a string. "I'll learn notes later," he said. "Like reading comes after talking." She sat with that for a second. It was the way anyone learned their own language, babbling and imitating long before any alphabet, and it had never once occurred to her that music could be entered the same way, mouth first, eyes second.

Mr. Popescu came in carrying a stack of folders and shooed the boy toward his mother, who was waiting in the hall. Then he looked at Naomi, who was still staring at the upside down page. "Something wrong?"

"No. I'm trying to figure out whether I'm jealous of him." She said it and heard how true it was. Her reading was fast and her ear, she suspected, was lazy, a muscle she'd let atrophy because the page always did that work for her. Abdul arrived then, unwinding his scarf, and dropped into the seat on her other side, complaining that the student council had become an oligarchy of five seniors who called every vote before anyone else spoke. Naomi laughed, but she filed the word away; it felt like it belonged to her current problem too, the way one narrow path to music had quietly taken over and called itself the only one.

"Jealous," Mr. Popescu repeated, tuning a school cello that had been left in a corner. "Of the playing or the not-reading?"

She hadn't separated those. During the rehearsal she kept thinking about it, missing her own entrance in the second movement because she was watching the boy's mother through the window, humming something in the hallway, the boy echoing her back note for note. When they broke for water, Abdul nudged her. "You're obdurate tonight. Third time he's had to point at your part." She apologized and put her eyes back on the page, and the page gave her the rhythm instantly, which was its own small mercy.

Afterward, packing up, she made a decision she didn't fully understand yet. She asked Saif to hum a phrase from the new piece, one she'd never seen, and she turned her music stand around so the page faced the wall. He hummed it twice, badly, and she reached into her memory for the shape of it, found only the edges, and played something wrong. She played it again. Wrong differently, but closer. Somewhere in her chest the uncertainty sat next to something that felt almost like delight, and she could not yet tell which one she was supposed to trust.

"One more time," she said to Saif. "Hum it again."

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
knowledge_domain: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
fact: An intersect overlay in GIS keeps only the areas that appear in both input layers, so intersecting housing with a flood zone shows just the homes inside the zone.
story:
The laptop Hudson had reserved at the public library was the one by the window, and when he sat down at four o'clock the sun came in low and turned the screen into a mirror of his own face, so the first thing he did was pull the blind halfway and prop his binder against the monitor. Inside the binder was everything he had collected since September: a printout of the city's flood zone map, a spreadsheet of housing assessments, and a letter from his grandmother's neighbour on Ferris Street, written in blue ballpoint, describing how the water had come to the second step of her porch in the spring. He was making this map for the ward meeting in eleven days. The councillor's aide had said they'd take five minutes of public comment, and Hudson intended to spend his five minutes showing, not telling.

Ms. Kapoor stopped at his table with a stack of returns balanced against her hip. "You're the one who asked about the GIS licence," she said. "It's installed on this machine and the two behind the reference desk. The tutorial files are in a folder called Training, and if it crashes, come find me instead of restarting it." She set down a granola bar beside his mouse, unopened, and kept walking before he could thank her. He turned it over once and put it in his bag for later.

The tutorial took him through layers, and he understood layers the way he understood transparencies on an old projector: the streets were one sheet, the flood zone another, the parcel data a third. He spent an hour digitizing, zooming until he could see the shape of his grandmother's lot, a small rectangle with a notch where the neighbour's fence cut in. When he finally got all three layers stacked, he ran his first overlay and sat back, satisfied, until the results appeared and every parcel in the entire city lit up in red. Fourteen thousand properties. He checked the layer list, unchecked and rechecked boxes, ran it again. Fourteen thousand properties, Ferris Street indistinguishable from the hillside subdivisions that had never seen water.

Nour slid into the chair across from him without asking, which was how Nour did most things. She was there for her own project, a survey of tree canopy in her neighbourhood that she'd been chasing since a heat wave in August sent her little brother to the hospital with heat exhaustion for an afternoon that she still described only in fragments. She wanted to prove to the city that her blocks had half the canopy of the ones three kilometres east, and she wanted the map finished before the next budget cycle, because money for trees, she said, moved slower than money for anything else.

"What's wrong with it," she said, looking at his screen. It wasn't a question. Hudson turned the laptop so she could see.

"It's showing every house in the city. I need only the ones in the flood zone."

"You used the wrong tool." She leaned in, tapping the toolbar. "Try intersect. An intersect keeps only the areas that appear in both layers, so when you intersect housing with the flood zone, you get just the homes inside the zone."

He found the tool and ran it, and the red fell away in a slow redraw, street by street, until only a long ragged band along the river stayed lit, and inside that band, small and bright, the notch-shaped lot on Ferris Street. He looked at it for a while before he said anything. "There they are," he said finally. "All of them."

Nour had already gone back to her own screen, but she glanced over when he said it. "How many?"

He opened the attribute table and counted the selected records. Two hundred and eleven parcels. He had walked that street in the spring and spoken to perhaps fifteen households, and he'd begun to think the problem was those fifteen, that the letter in blue ballpoint stood for a street. He understood now that he had been thinking too small and also too randomly at once, that his fifteen interviews had been happenstance rather than method, a sample shaped by whose doors happened to open.

Gurleen arrived at five with her headphones around her neck and the specific energy of someone who had spent the day being told she was too young to care about zoning. She was on the environmental committee at school with Hudson, and she'd come to help him compile the flood records, though she had her own reasons, which she announced while unpacking her laptop: her family's insurance had gone up thirty percent this year, and no one at the company would explain why, and she'd started to suspect that what the insurer called risk and what the city called risk were two different maps drawn by two different hands. She wanted to see if the city's map agreed with anything at all.

They worked until the light outside went from gold to grey, and Hudson found himself caught between two instincts. Gurleen wanted him to argue that the concentration of older, cheaper housing inside the flood band was endemic to the way the city had approved development, a pattern rather than an accident, and to say so at the meeting. Nour, who had watched three presentations to council die on the strength of their claims, wanted him to show the map and stop talking. "Show the two hundred and eleven parcels," she said. "Say which tool you used. Let them impugn their own data if they want to."

"They'll say the model's outdated," Gurleen said.

"Then they'll say it," Nour said. "That's their problem, not yours."

Hudson saved the project twice, onto the desktop and onto the USB drive in his pocket, and printed the map at the reference desk in colour, which cost him the last of his card balance. Ms. Kapoor came over to clear the paper jam, and while she worked the drawer she looked at the printout for a long moment, the river's band and the bright parcels inside it. "Ferris Street," she said. "My aunt lived there before the bypass went in. She used to say the water remembered where it used to go." She handed him the warm page and tapped the granola bar still poking out of his bag. "Eat that before you bike home. It's a long ride in the dark."

He folded the map along the river line and put it in his binder with the blue ballpoint letter, and Gurleen held the door while Nour, already composing an email to the urban forestry office under the streetlight, walked out backwards into the evening. "Eleven days," she said. "You'll be ready."

Hudson got on his bike, the map's crease pressed flat under the binder clip. "Two hundred and eleven," he said, and pushed off down the hill.

activity: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
knowledge_domain: to debate a current issue entirely in a new language for five minutes
fact: Aristotle named three means of persuasion: ethos, the speaker's credibility; pathos, the audience's emotions; and logos, the logic of the argument.
story:
The topic went up on the whiteboard in Ms. Zhu's careful characters: should cities make public transit free? Isaac copied it into his notebook, and beneath it, in English, he wrote five minutes, and the words looked like a sentence being handed down. On Thursday each of them would stand and argue the issue entirely in Mandarin, no notes, no stopping. Five minutes was nothing in English. In Mandarin it was a country he had a visa for but no map of.

He had prepared the way he prepared for everything, which was to say he had made lists. Free transit reduces congestion. Free transit costs money that must come from somewhere. Drivers switch modes when fares drop. Subsidies favor the poor. He had translated each point with a dictionary app, drilled the vocabulary on the bus, and by Tuesday he could recite the whole ladder of reasoning in tones that were, if not perfect, at least consistent. He practiced on Jaime in the back row of the language lab, and Jaime listened with his chin in his hand, tapping the desk.

"You sound like a textbook," Jaime said, in English, because the practice had ended and honesty was allowed again. "Every sentence is a claim with a citation." He rummaged in his bag and pulled out a wrinkled handout from the debate club he'd quit in tenth grade. "Remember this? Aristotle. Ethos, pathos, logos." He flattened the page against the desk. "Credibility, emotion, logic. The three means of persuasion." Isaac looked at the three Greek words and felt something in his chest tilt, the way a shelf tilts when you finally notice the weight has always been on one side.

Every point he had was logos. All fifteen of his careful sentences were logic, stacked like bricks, and a wall of bricks alone did not persuade anyone of anything, because persuasion was not the same as being right. He remembered being thirteen and arguing with his father about moving schools, producing statistic after statistic about the new district's rankings, and his father finally saying, quietly, that Isaac had never once asked what he was afraid of. Isaac had thought he'd lost the argument on a technicality. Now he wasn't sure he had been in an argument at all.

On Wednesday evening he sat at the kitchen table and tried to build the other two floors. Ethos, credibility: who was he to speak about transit? He was a boy who rode the 42 every morning, packed in with nurses and students and a man who sold phone chargers out of a duffel bag. That could be said in Mandarin. He had the words for morning, for crowded, for five years. Pathos was harder. He thought of Belle, who had missed a midterm in October because her bus fare had gone to her younger brother's inhaler and she'd walked the eight kilometers, arriving with her hair soaked and her exam half blank. She'd told the story lightly, laughing at herself, and everyone had laughed with her, and Isaac had laughed too, and only later understood that the lightness was the whole point of the telling.

He asked Belle after class if he could use it, translating his request into halting Mandarin first because Ms. Zhu was near, then giving up and switching. "Not to cajole the class," he said. "Just so they feel the number behind the policy." Belle considered it, picking at the strap of her bag. "Say I walked," she said. "Don't say why. If you explain it, it's just your logic again." That was a subtlety he would not have arrived at alone, that emotion argued best when it pretended not to be arguing.

Thursday came and Ms. Zhu called his name. His first minute was the brick wall, the statistics, delivered at speed so that his tones could not waver. Then he paused, which he had not planned, and said that every morning he rode the 42, and that among the passengers was a girl who one day in October walked eight kilometers and arrived too late. He watched a girl in the second row stop writing. He watched Jaime nod once. He did not explain what the inhaler had cost or what the midterm had meant, because Belle had told him not to, and in the gap where the explanation would have been, the room went quiet and stayed that way.

In his final minute he tried to bring the two halves together, the fares and the walking, and found he could not make them agree. The numbers said a free system would be slow and expensive and possibly worse than what it replaced; the story said that the girl had still walked. He ended, thirty seconds early, on the sentence he had decided at two in the morning was the only honest one: that he did not know, and that perhaps the city did not know either. He stood there with his hands at his sides, having argued himself into the open.

Ms. Zhu gave him a score he did not look at until he sat down. It was the lowest in the class. "Very moving," she said to the room, in Mandarin, marking her clipboard. "But a debate requires a conclusion. Next time, choose a side." Isaac slid the paper into his notebook. Beside him, Jaime leaned over and whispered, in careful, disastrous tones, "Wo bu zhidao," and shrugged, and grinned.
